speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to move a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Whereas, the unilateral action taken by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) to increase the St. Lawrence seaway tolls will seriously and adversely affect our export trade, Canada-United States relations, primary and secondary industries including therein steel, agriculture and coal, to name a few, and will inflict
severe irreparable economic hardship on the city of Hamilton and district and over all will increase unemployment.
And whereas, at least the provinces of Ontario, Alberta, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the Canadian Labour Congress and the Canadian Seafarers' International Union and many others are unilaterally opposed to any increase in tolls. 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling):
That the issues of the St. Lawrence seaway and financial implications related thereto be referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications for the purposes of identifying the number of direct and indirect economic inter-relationships that exist with respect to the usage of the seaway and further determining whether the raising of tolls is in the best interests of Canada and until a report from the said committee is tabled and reviewed that no further action be taken to introduce a new tariff of tolls.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: SASKATCHEWAN URANIUM REFINERY SITE
speechtext:
Eldorado Nuclear Limited has publicly
announced that it has acquired options to purchase 1,200 acres near Warman, Saskatchewan, so that detailed environmental studies can be conducted to determine whether the site would be suitable for a uranium refinery. These studies will begin in early 1977, and because of their comprehensive nature must examine a wide range of environmental factors over four seasons. The results of these studies will be published in the spring of 1978 in the form of an Environmental Impact Statement, as required by the environmental assessment guidelines and criteria established by the Governments of Canada and Saskatchewan. Both Governments also require that the Environmental Impact Statements be subject to public hearings, and that the public be given ample opportunity to examine the complete assessment documentation prior to the public hearings. The approval process is expected to take upwards of six months. During this period, the Company must also complete its evaluation of the amount and metallurgical nature of the potential supply of concentrates from new uranium mine-mill operations in the northern part of Saskatchewan, and reassess at that time the potential markets for refined uranium products. Therefore, because of all these factors the Company will not be in a position until the latter part of 1978, at the earliest, to announce whether it will proceed with applications to various authorities, including the Atomic Energy Control Board, for authority to construct a refinery at Warman.

speechtext:
I am informed by the Departments of the Environment, Industry, Trade and Commerce and Supply and Services as follows: 1. As a matter of policy, the Department of the Environment supports waste paper and other materials re-cycling, as a means of conserving energy and other resources; as a way to lessen total environmental impacts; and does so in all cases where it has been shown that these benefits occur.
2 and 3. The government has not given direct incentives to either the paper industry or to buyers. However, the government has provided indirect incentives, by eliminating the federal sales tax on equipment and materials used by the commercial processors and re-cyclers of reclaimed waste paper.
4.	No export markets have yet been determined specifically for re-cycied paper, however, waste paper is used as a portion of the fibre furnished by some newsprint manufacturers. speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: LEVELS AT WHICH RADIOACTIVE FALLOUT IS CONSIDERED HARMFUL
speechtext: Does the government or any of its agencies, set specific levels in Canada at which radioactive fallout is considered harmful to the public, wildlife or domestic animals and, if so (a) what are the levels (b) do the levels differ from those specified by the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: LEVELS AT WHICH RADIOACTIVE FALLOUT IS CONSIDERED HARMFUL
speechtext:
(a) Radiation at any level is considered harmful in some degree. However, fallout is not subject to domestic control at source and the available counter-measures carry their own adverse health consequences. Therefore, protective actions must be based on a balancing of risks. Radiological health effects depend on the physical and chemical characteristics of the radioactive element involved, their mode of entry into the body and their deposition and retention in specific organs. For tropospheric fallout, iodine-131 is the element of greatest concern; for stratospheric fallout, the concern is chiefly with strontium-90. For both, the principal mode of entry into the body is by the consumption of milk. The amount taken into the body via other foods, drinking water and air is relatively small. The maximum permissible levels in milk, as derived from the recommendations of the International Commission on Radiological Protection, are 2,000 picocuries of iodine-131 per litre and 400 picocuries of strontium-90 per litre. The corresponding maximum permissible levels in air are 300 picocuries of iodine-131 per cubic metre and 40 picocuries of strontium-90 per cubic metre. For the complex mixture of radionuclides in fresh fallout in air, it is estimated that the equivalent level for gross beta radio-activity is about 2,500 picocuries per cubic metre. On this basis, it is considered that for short-term transient fallout exposures, levels in milk should not exceed the above value. However, if a period of widespread, long-term fallout was in prospect, more restrictive levels, approximately W of the above, would be specified to conform with the recommendation of the International Commission on Radiological Protection relating to the continuous exposure of a whole population, (b) The relevant United States levels are expressed in different terms, but in application do not differ significantly. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has recommended graded scales of action if the total intake of a radionuclide from air, water and food falls within certain ranges. Range III, which requires consideration of possible counter-measures (other than surveillance), is 100-1,000 picocuries per day for iodine-131 and 200-2,000 picocuries

per day for strontium-90. These levels relate to average intakes by members of a sample population and they may be further averaged over a period of one year to allow for transient fluctuations.

subsubtopic: ACTION IF RADIOACTIVE FALLOUT LEVELS BECOME DANGEROUSLY HIGH
speechtext: What action, if any, does the government consider it necessary that should be taken if radioactive fallout levels become dangerously high in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: ACTION IF RADIOACTIVE FALLOUT LEVELS BECOME DANGEROUSLY HIGH
speechtext: If the level of iodine-131 in milk reached the level at which countermeasures became necessary, liquid milk would be withdrawn from the market and substituted by powdered milk which had been produced prior to the appearance of fresh fallout or which had been stored for a length of time sufficient to allow the short lived iodine-131 to decay. The permissible level for strontium-90 would not be reached unless there was continued nuclear weapons testing for a long time. Strontium 90 can be removed from milk by central processing. Technically, the treatment is not difficult, but its application on a national scale would involve very great expense.

The House resumed, from Wednesday, March 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Basford (for the Minister of Transport) that Bill C-33, to amend the National Transportation Act and the Department of Transport Act for the purpose of defining the objective of the transportation policy of Canada and authorizing the consequential rearrangement of powers and duties relating to transport and to amend the Transport Act and the Railway Act in respect of freight rates and other matters, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the debate ended yesterday I had a few brief moments in which to commence my remarks concerning the national transportation bill. At that time, having heard several members who sometimes support the government in this House deplore the fact that the government is reneging-and having listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) with respect to their $290 million commitment to help urban transit in this country-I invited the Minister of Finance, who 1 hope will accept this invitation, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), and other members who are now trying to get on the right side of this issue to turn up at the Toronto Union station at 8 a.m. on March 14 to see first-hand the congestion that exists in the metropolitan Toronto area as far as commuters are concerned. That invitation does not come just from me; it also comes from the regional chairmen in that area who are sending wires to most of the affected members of this House asking them to join with those chairmen on Monday morning, March 14, to see first-hand the situation that this government is helping to leave in the Toronto area concerning commuter travel.
For the record, I should read the telegram that is being sent out by Paul Godfrey, chairman of the Metropolitan Toronto council. The telegram reads:
Deep concern over the federal announcement that funds for urban transit are not to be made available. Request you to join me and the regional chairmen from the regions surrounding metro on Monday, March 14 at 8 a.m. at the Union station GO transit platform. We will at that time wish to discuss with you the effect the broken federal promise will have on all of us.
March 3, 1977

That shows the anxiety that now exists in the Toronto area concerning this very important matter. If I may, 1 would like very quickly to summarize where the uncertainty first arose. As most in this House realize, during the 1974 election campaign the Liberal party, seeking re-election as the government of this country, spewed forth much in the way of promises to help their way back into office. Included in those promises were very specific commitments concerning the assistance they were willing to give urban transit authorities in our various metropolitan areas. They even put a price tag on it. They said that the promises would probably represent about $290 million of federal assistance. The short fact is that government did get re-elected. Presumably those promises helped them to get re-elected. Now that they are in office with a majority, they are simply reneging on the promises they made to the Canadian electorate.
I say they reneged for this reason. I grant that there is a bit of confusion about this, but we find, in answer to questions put by my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), and myself, that the Minister of Finance on February 18 confirmed remarks he presumably made at a press conference the day before. For example, he stated, and I quote from page 3184 of Hansard:
-the federal government will not be able to extend its assistance to municipalities which we had hoped to assist in earlier years.
That, of course, refers to the question of funding for urban transit. As a result of that type of question I asked the minister whether he had ridden on the commuter train at rush hour going into the Toronto area in order to experience first-hand the congestion of that service. There was no meaningful comment on that, so I again reiterate the question and invite the Minister of Finance, along with his Prime Minister, to share, with other members of parliament and the local chairmen in the Toronto area, the experience of seeing how commuters in that area are now being handled because of the lack of forethought and funding for which the federal government is responsible.
Subsequent to that comment by the Minister of Finance, some confusion came into this question. In response to a question put by myself to the Prime Minister on February 25 concerning why he felt free to break his promise with regard to urban funding, the Prime Minister stated:
There has been no decision one way or another but we are keeping the various arguments in mind-
So it would appear there is hope the government may yet come to its senses. It might make the Minister of Finance look a little foolish; he spoke out of turn and he certainly did not speak wisely. I hope that whatever the background is, the goverment will acknowledge that it does have outstanding commitments to the public and that for the sake of commuters in the Montreal area, in the Toronto area, the areas of Vancouver, Edmonton and Calgary and other urban centres in this country which face pressing transit problems, it will live up to those commitments.
National Transportation Act
The confusion goes even deeper. Here we have a promise made in 1974. The Minister of Finance says, in effect, that the government cannot meet the promise, that it must renege. Then we find there are estimates before the House tabled by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), and when we look at page 2762 of those estimates we see, under the heading "Urban Transit" that an expenditure of $8,136,000 is contemplated by the federal government. 1 ask this question: Who is running the show? Who, exactly, knows on any day of the week what the government intends to do with regard to this question-and, presumably, with regard to many others? Why is the government being asked to approve an expenditure of $8,136,000 in relation to urban transit when the Minister of Finance tells us there is no money available to spend on urban transportation? We are entitled to an explanation.
I see the Minister of Transport sitting in his place. I am glad he has the nerve to come here. I think he should explain, after I have sat down, why he as Minister of Transport tolerated the Minister of Finance telling us there is no money available for urban transportation while his own estimate for $8,136,000 is before the House and will, presumably, be passed unless it is defeated at some stage of the parliamentary process. In short, the government seems to be in a dither. I believe it is time an assurance was given to the various provinces and municipalities that Ottawa is willing to help out by providing some of the funding needed to ensure that those who must travel to and from work can do so by the most effective means, which is a suitable system of urban transportation.
When I speak on this subject I do so with a strong sense of deja vu. Unlike the Johnies-come-lately on the government back-benches who are only now beginning to understand the extend of the government's failure in the field of urban transit policy, we in this party have consistently pressed for common sense in this vital area. On no fewer than 90 occasions have we spoken in the House against Pickering airport. On more than 20 of those occasions I have put questions to successive ministers of transport with a view to persuading them to drop the ill-advised Pickering project and redirecting any unused funds to urban assistance. In fact, in my first speech in the House, made at the time the government could have saved many millions of dollars by shelving the Pickering airport proposal-I refer to a speech made on January 12, 1973-I put the dilemma facing the Toronto area as simply as possible. As recorded at page 251 of Hansard, I stated:
On behalf of those people let me tell the government once again, we do not need a second airport at Pickering. We do need, however, federal assistance to facilitate urban transportation.
The same is true today. Despite the promises of the Prime Minister and of no less than four ministers in his cabinet, there has been no substantial contribution to urban transportation in Toronto. In fact, the total federal government's contribution to date in Ontario has been one $10 million grant to cover rolling stock for the Richmond Hill GOline. In contrast, Ontario has spent nearly $429 million since 1964 to support urban transit. Beyond that, the provincial municipalities have spent $90 million annually to meet their transit needs.

March 3, 1977
National Transportation Act
Clearly, the government is turning its back on the 75 per cent of our population who live in Canadian urban centres. On the other hand, the same government has spent more than $110 million for land development and management at Pickering, and has lost an additional $130 million in two years at Mirabel, despite the fact that only about 10 per cent of the population use airports on any regular basis. When I say 10 per cent of our population, Mr. Speaker, I must qualify that statement by saying that I have removed from that calculation the Minister of Transport's travels in and out of our airports, in order to put the figure in a more meaningful context.
The Minister of Transport tells us that urban transit is the domain of the provinces and is the responsibility of the provinces and the municipalities. Yet we find as far back as May 15, 1973, in my first private member's bill, a recommendation to establish a national urban transportation authority which, though funded partly by the federal authorities, would have the power to establish local urban or regional transportation authorities. I refer again to the situation, as 1 did then, in the United States, Great Britain, France and other countries where local or urban authorities oversee the local harbours, airports, interurban rail transportation and all transit needs within their purview. If such authorities existed in Canada there would no doubt be a completely different range of priorities to that now being shown by the government.
One important fact often forgotten is that where there are local authorities which not only look after transit in urban areas but also look after airports, harbours and similar services, such authorities are extremely conscious of the needs of the area and of the cost consequences of their actions. New York is one example. This is why in Chicago or New York, they would not dare propose to build a Mirabel or a Pickering airport at the present time. If you spoke to the officials of those authorities you would find them saying, first of all, that there is no evidence of public travel needs rising to the point at which additional facilities on this scale are needed in those centres and, in the second place, they would say they cannot afford the cost. They would explain that they cannot afford to build new airports because those airports could only be financed by getting the airline carriers to sign sufficient longterm commitments to cover the costs of construction and operation.
This approach is significantly different from the one adopted in Canada. Unfortunately, the entire process is centralized here in Ottawa in the Department of Transport, with one little brain trying to run the entire show. The fact is that this little brain cannot possibly cope with the variety of needs which exist in our urban centres as far as transportation is concerned and, consequently, a lot of mistakes are made. Mistakes are made because bureaucracies like to build monuments to themselves. They have a Taj Mahal complex. They like to be able to build something, touch it and say that Mirabel is there because they thought it was a good idea. The fact that Mirabel was not needed is a secondary thing. The fact that for years and years Canadians are going to have to pay needless interest and

operating costs to handle Mirabel is a secondary thing in their minds.
That brings me to the situation in Toronto. If there has been a co-ordinated local authority attitude taken in Toronto, the concept of a Pickering airport development before the commuter rail situation had been solved would not have been seriously advanced. The fact is that the local Toronto people realize that the No. 1 need in that area is to facilitate workers coming to and from work in a more humane way than that which exists at the present time. It is as simple as that. This government, centralized in Ottawa and acting under a minister who really does not understand, seems to accept the bureaucratic "build a monument" concept and says that we must have a Pickering. I am saying that money could be better spent developing proper urban transport facilities in the Toronto area, and the notion that a second airport is needed in that area is silly.
There are other ridiculous examples of where this minister and his predecessor, either directly or through agencies reporting to them, have done foolish things in Toronto with regard to priorities. For example, if the ministers choose to join us in the Toronto area on March 14, one of the things I hope they will sense is the congestion which exists at Union station. There are about 37,000 passengers going through Union station who use the rail service, and frankly Union station was not built to handle that many people. When the bilevel trains start in a few months it is likely that the congestion will be much greater. We need a new facility or some type of new transit facility to handle the crowds coming into Union station. That takes tens of millions of dollars to build. The federal government joined in the preliminary discussions with respect to that facility, but now, after those discussions have taken place, the government says there is no money to help facilitate the building.
On the question of priorities, why did the government allow the CN to build the CN tower which cost approximately $58 million and which will not make money in a meaningful way, when the very commuters who come to and from work every day in that city have to go by that tower and be subjected to congestion at Union station? Surely it is a ridiculous sense of priority to say that building the CN tower for $58 million should come before a decent facility to allow 37,000 people to come and go by way of rail transit which they choose to use.
Let me give another example. Not only is the rail station congested, but in the railyard itself the local GO transit authority cannot bring in additional trains from the west side of Toronto until there is a realignment of the trackage. Incidentally, that trackage goes right by the CN tower. It will cost approximately $57 million to realign that trackage, but here again priority was given to building the CN tower before the federal government was willing to spend money on trackage which is impeding further commuter lines coming in from the west side of Toronto. That is unbelievable.
However, clearly the only reason these inconsistencies occur in the Toronto area is that this minister, his predecessor, the
March 3, 1977

government and the Prime Minister do not know what they are doing in relation to the Toronto problem. For example, with absolutely no reference to the Toronto area they chose to propose the Toronto waterfront park. They went ahead and bought that land. They did not ask the mayor of Toronto or the chairman of the metropolitan Toronto region if they felt the park would be a nice thing, or whether it was needed. They did not ask whether that was a priority or whether they should be spending money on that before helping people get to and from work.
They went ahead and bought it and, most alarmingly, when they are now questioned as to why they had money for the Toronto harbour front-and yet now they say, in relation to their 1974 promises concerning urban transit, that they do not have the $290 million to help with urban transit-what are we told? The President of the Treasury Board has the audacity to say in this House that the Toronto waterfront project was a 1972 promise, and he grinned, implying that the 1974 promises do not count. That is the mentality of this government. That is the mentality which has caused millions of Canadians to lose confidence in this government. They want to get rid of this government as quickly as possible.
I have outlined this, but perhaps for those who are not willing to take my word I shall read into the record an editorial comment in the Toronto Star of February 22. Under the headline "Ottawa makes chaos for commuters" this article reads in part as follows:
Every day 37,000 rail passengers, mostly commuters, pass through a congested and antiquated Union station. It's clear to everyone of them, although not to transport minister Otto Lang in Ottawa, that the place was designed for a more leisurely era.
A bigger crush is yet to come. This fall the first of 80 new double-decker trains will appear on the Lakeshore GO transit line, running between Oakville and Pickering, boosting capacity from 28,000 passengers a day to 42,000 a day.
Union Station was to have had better tracks and wider platforms before the new coaches and additional passengers started arriving. But Ottawa's backtracking on its 1974 election promise to aid urban transit means it's unlikely the station will be expanded or the angle of railway tracks at Bathurst St. will be straightened out. Ottawa's refusal to keep its word is creating commuter chaos in metro.
This is an urgent problem. I am pleased that certain Liberal backbenchers who like to support the government are at least guardedly speaking and pointing out to the government that it is making a mistake. 1 hope they will have the courage to vote against this bill when the vote is taken at second reading. 1 also hope that if this bill is defeated, the Prime Minister will regard that as a vote of no confidence in his government and that he will resign.

The "on again, off again" promises of the Prime Minister lead us to ask just who is speaking for the government. Is it the Minister of Transport, the Prime Minister, or the Minister of Finance?
I know my colleagues want to participate in this debate, and I wish I had more time. I would like to have read into the
National Transportation Act
record the promises which were made to the Canadian public in the 1974 election campaign concerning urban transit. Perhaps tomorrow as this debate continues, or on our own opposition motion, there will be opportunities to read some of those promises into the record.
However, those broken promises in all likelihood spell an end to $200 million of transit projects in the metropolitan Toronto area. They spell an end to the $57 million of upgrading and renovation of Union station, which I have referred to. They spell an end to the $25 million of extension on the Streetsville GO line. Also, they will spell an end to the $80 million of light rail line construction to the Scarborough town centre.

speechtext: What about Montreal?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
They will spell an end to the $35 million purchase of rail cars for the Lakeshore GO system. Someone asked, "What about Montreal?" Montreal has a problem, too, and this federal government has failed to acknowledge the problem. 1 have the honour to represent an area just north of metropolitan Toronto and I feel that I have the right to stand in this House and point out the inadequacies of federal policy in regard to the Toronto transit situation. I would welcome it if the hon. member would stand in the House and speak in favour of more urban transit for people in Montreal and let the federal government know in no uncertain terms that Montreal, too, is being short-changed by a federal government that thinks more of its own political power than of serving the Canadian public.
I have referred to the fact that there has been a reneging on the part of the government in regard to urban transit promises. But it goes further than that. In our type of federation there must be great trust between the federal government, the ten provinces and the territories. When deals are made, those deals must be honoured. I think it is most reprehensible that a deal was made, for example, by the Minister of Transport's predecessor, now Senator Marchand, in which he gave an assurance-indeed, a commitment-to the Ontario government that if they wished to go ahead and buy 80 bilevel cars which they would order from Hawker Siddeley in Thunder Bay at a cost of approximately $38 million, the federal government would pay the cost of that purchase. Now the federal government is reneging.
If any member on the other side of this House doubts what I say, I would refer him to the statement in the legislature of Ontario made by the hon. James Snow, minister of transportation and communications, on December 16 of last year. He was quite clear. He pointed out in no uncertain terms that Ontario had made plans based on firm commitments given by federal authorities, and those commitments were apparently not going to be honoured. He further stated that he had had a meeting with the Minister of Transport and that he hoped the Minister of Transport would come back to him and show some realization of the situation and agree that the commitments would be honoured. He anticipated, as he spoke in the legisla-

March 3, 1977
National Transportation Act
ture, that he would hear from the Minister of Transport before Christmas of last year.
The fact is that to this point the Ontario government has not heard from the Minister of Transport, or from anybody else at the ministerial level in the government, in regard to these outstanding commitments in connection with the purchase to which the Ontario government has committed itself. I would recommend to any hon. member who wishes to join in this debate, particularly if he is on the government side, to take a look at the statement made by Mr. Snow in the Ontario legislature which vividly shows the uncertainty now existing between the Ontario authorities and the federal government over urban transit in the Toronto area at the present time-in fact, throughout Ontario.
I am pleased to have had the opportunity to make a few comments on the bill before the House. The important thing we must bear in mind is that if we are not careful, the highly centralized control which we have in the Ministry of Transport will not be responsive to the needs of the various cities and regions within this country to the extent it should be. The minister likes to say that he is evolving a policy of user-pay. There is nothing wrong with the concept. But when you start to analyse it, Mr. Speaker, you ask: User pay what? Who decides whether an operation is being run efficiently? Who decides if a Mirabel should be built and consequently paid for? Is it fair to talk to Canadians about user-pay, for example, in the case of a Mirabel or in the case of the operation of the Toronto international airport No. 1 or the proposed No. 2? Is it fair to say the user should pay when there is absolutely no control on the expenditure side with respect to what those users are being asked to pay? That, Mr. Speaker, can only be decided by the vote of the Canadian public.
In short, what is the point of the Minister of Transport saying that he has got a new theory, that users are going to start paying for services that are under his control, when there is serious doubt whether those services are, first of all, in many cases needed; and, secondly, are being run in an efficient way that warrants the user-pay concept?
More than that, Mr. Speaker, when you are in government there is never any question of who pays: it is the taxpayer who pays. All the minister is saying is that he would like to take from one group of taxpayers and give to another group and say that the users are paying. My point is that it is all very fine to talk of user-pay provided you can show that the government has acted in a frugal way, that they have moved only to build the facilities that are needed in a particular area.
Unfortunately, we have one of the saddest transport departments, in Canada, of any comparable country in the world. The government builds monuments to civil servants and then expects Canadians, either through their tax dollars or through their usage of services, to pay, and in many cases to pay for services that are needless. It is time that those who have supported the government to date showed their mettle. If they want to be re-elected in the Toronto area, then let them stand up, show a little courage and vote against this bill.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the members on both sides who have participated in this debate so far, and I think that with the exception of the opposition critic practically the entire debate has been taken up generally with the problems of metro Toronto and other metropolitan areas in this country. While I fully realize there are such problems and that there is a delineation of responsibility between the federal government, the provinces and the municipalities, I suggest there are many other issues in other parts of the country that are equally important and which will be affected by the legislation which is before us today.
Bill C-33 is a very major bill which is of interest to every member of the House no matter which region he represents or to which particular party he belongs. I think the amendments proposed will go quite a distance in meeting many of the concerns that have been expressed, not only in this debate but in the House over the last number of years-almost daily in the question period-with regard to affairs of transport. I am quite sure the bill will not provide a framework which will solve all our transportation problems.
The general topic of transportation policy, the lack of it, the results of it, have been a favourite political whipping-boy for a very long time, and in many cases with good reason. I think yesterday we had pretty good evidence of that. Some of the shenanigans which went on in the House underline the concern of hon. members or this particular issue. Certainly, both political groups and other special interest groups will as well, I am sure, keep the issue before the government for some time in the future.
Some of the points I want to comment upon are related to achievements and to the progress which has definitely been made over the last few years in western Canada. Many changes have been made and a good deal of progress has been made to alleviate some of the long-standing sore points so far as western Canada is concerned. I am the first to say that by no means have we exhausted the list as yet, nor can this legislation provide answers to all those concerns.
It was less than ten years ago, as was mentioned by one hon. member participating in the debate, that this House extensively debated the present National Transportation Act which was adopted under a minority government. I am sure it had the support of the majority of members at that time, and I am sure they thought, also, that it would take care of the transportation needs and would form a framework for transportation policies for many years to come. That was only eight years ago. I am sure hon. members were satisfied then that they had the correct legislation and the correct regulatory mechanism basically in place to deal with those problems.
That act was the result of the MacPherson Commission study which had been at work for many years prior to that. The events leading up to some of these changes at which we are looking in Bill C-33 are worth noting. The former minister of transport-referred to by the hon. member who just
March 3, 1977

resumed his seat-recognized the difficulties faced by him, by the government and by this country in his now famous remark to the effect that the transportation policy of Canada was a mess, a remark which was widely publicized and, I might say, widely misinterpreted.
The former minister certainly, was not being critical, as was the hon. member who just resumed his seat, of the thousands of dedicated people in the Department of Transport and in other agencies across this country who work, and have worked hard, to provide good transportation services of which we can be proud instead of continually criticizing it. I do not say that there is no room for improvement, but everyone seems to criticize our two major railroads. It is a toss-up between them and the CBC as to which is more of a politicial whipping-boy. But the fact is that those two major railroads, despite the odds of geography and severe winter weather and other difficulties with which they have to contend in Canada, get the job done in a remarkable way.
The changes that took place since the 1967 act brought about a review of policy and a review of programs and another look at the legislation, which led up to the introduction of Bill C-33 in the House in this session. For example, in the eight years since the present act came into force we have seen dramatic change. We have seen growth in the demand for and the price of our resources such as oil, grain, potash and coal, all of which place significantly increased pressure on the capacity of our transportation system in the first instance. Second, we are all aware, and, are becoming more aware every day, of the energy crisis which sharpens our awareness of the need to conserve energy. The change of attitudes and values resulting in our concern about growth rates and the environmental impact of the Mackenzie Valley pipeline, which is a major transportation issue, and the study on that, are a reflection of that fact.
Certainly, there are significant advances in transportation technology in a variety of fields too numerous to mention. Those are some of the changing trends and changing patterns that have developed in this country and are part of life today which perhaps were not so obvious a mere eight years ago when the former act was in place. It was the variety of policies and programs that had grown up in different parts of the country to meet different situations that had in some cases changed from the time they were first initiated, and this was the kind of thing that led the former minister to make the statement that he made that the transportation policy is in a mess and should be reviewed.
There was a growth in size of some of our very large agencies, usually accompanied by a growth in independence as a result, and that has been a trend in government-federal, provincial and others. Bill C-33 proposes to make the arrangements between the major regulatory body in this act-namely, the CTC-and the minister's office, the minister's powers and duties, a good deal more flexible than is now the case under the present legislation. The rate-regulating side of the CTC remains unchanged in principle, but policy and research functions should be primarily an MOT responsibility and the
National Transportation Act
responsibility of the minister in charge. He is charged with those responsibilities; he is held accountable here in the House and across the country-and consequently he should have the authority in those fields.
As I have said, there have been a good few noteworthy improvements and achievements in recent years, despite the continued criticism and continued concerns coming from all parts of the country on transportation matters. In western Canada, so far as our grievances are concerned-and many of them have been there since confederation-a number of points are well worth noting. First of all, and perhaps most important, it seems to me that in the last two or three years we are learning more about the nature of those specific grievances. By hollering about high freight rates and generalities of that kind we will not change them. There are great distances to cover.
We are, indeed, captive shippers in so far as the railways are concerned, in the great majority of cases. We are learning more about those problems. We are identifying them and spelling them out more clearly. We are consulting with a great many more people involved. I am not talking just about the users, about the industries and about the unions and the people involved in providing the services. I am talking about the provincial governments and other governments involved and affected by transportation policies. The work of the former minister in initiating and setting up federal-provincial groups and committees in western Canada, in the maritimes, in Quebec and in Ontario-which practice has been developed and maintained by the present minister-has in itself gone a long way to help alleviate some of those problems by setting up a better consultative mechanism. As I say, in my view that has been a significant achievement in the last several years. Provincial governments today are much more closely involved than they were a mere four or five years ago.
Another move that was made by this government a year or so ago was to pass legislation forcing the railroad to provide its costs on specific rates and charges to the federal government on a confidential basis, which would then be made available to the provinces. Certainly this is working well and is enabling us to get answers to some of the concerns which were discussed earlier in the debate by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin). We are getting more of the answers now.
We have been able to substantiate some of the facts. Bill C-33 will eliminate the long-haul short-haul anomaly that has long been not only a sore spot with western Canadians but a good deal worse than that. There is provision for certain exceptions which I hope the minister will deal with when the bill goes to committee. I realize that there are valid reasons for the flexibility being there and I hope the minister can elaborate on that when the bill goes to committee.
The reduction of the maximum rate is another move which I think will work to the advantage of all Canadians, particularly western Canadians. That amendment is contained in the bill. Hopper cars were mentioned in the earlier remarks of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), in the absence of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), as being another develop-

March 3, 1977
National Transportation Act
ment and advance in transportation in western Canada. This is not covered by the bill, but it is one of those achievements which, as I mentioned, has taken place over the last several years. We should not assume, as we might from listening to some of the arguments advanced by hon. members, that we can completely reject the economic facts of life, and transportation is nothing more nor less than pure political posturing. The minister and the government have not said, nor did they ever say, that all transportation services must be economical.
What we have said, and what has been the policy and practice for many years-and certainly a very defensible one-is that we must ensure we are carefully spending the money and the funds, that are going to support the many special exceptions to the basic rule. The user, in the majority of cases, still must pay for services rendered. The transportation policy and this legislation will enable the minister and the government to ensure it now becomes a more effective government tool for alleviating regional disparities and promoting regional economic development. I think that is one of the criticisms that has been put forward, not only from the west but from the east and other parts of the country, that will in essence enable the minister and the government to respond to this concern.
There have been two or three other achievements over the past few years. In western Canada we are awaiting the Hall commission report dealing with the question of branch lines. We hope that will be handed down before long and will give us some direction. The Snaveley report on grain handling is another transportation-oriented issue. We are learning the real facts, and any time we come up with that result we will be able more sensibly to deal with the issues it provides for better resolution of the problems. There are still very many valid concerns in western Canada regarding transportation, and today we are delineating more of them, in co-operation with provincial governments and other groups, than we have for many years. We understand much better the nature of the problem.
The bill will go a long way, but of course it will not resolve our concerns although it will provide a better framework to deal with those issues and concerns. Transportation is a very important aspect of the social life of all of us, so important to the community and the economy, both domestically and in terms of linking us with our markets, that we cannot afford as a government to become less involved. I think that if need be we should become more involved. These amendments will provide that opportunity.
The amendments make it clear that the regulatory function which is necessary for the proper management of Canadian transportation-the Canadian Transport Commission will continue in that role with less emphasis on legal procedures and with more administrative simplicity. The amendments will ensure that the Minister of Transport and his department is the principal source of transportation policy advice to the government. They will give the minister and the government a

more acceptable means of giving policy direction to the CTC itself, but not in the context of any specific case that may be before the commission.
The government has made a good deal of progress in the last several years. Both the former minister and the present minister and their staff have devoted a great deal of effort and energy to the job. I am sure some of my hon. friends opposite will not agree, but 1 can certainly say that the minister has been tackling many of the problems in a very capable manner. The problems that have been plaguing the country for many years are not going to disappear simply because they are not recognized-problems compounded by inflation and the changing concerns of people and by working with policies and institutions that are not amenable to change.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is not the first time parliament has engaged in a debate on the principles of the transportation system of our country. Some of us remember the great hopes we had from the Duff report in the 1930s when it was recommended that the railways of the country, particularly on the prairies, be rationalized in their operation to overcome the mistakes of the early development period. After the war the problem was still with us. Then in 1949-50 we had the Turgeon royal commission. Once again, the commission made the same recommendation, that we should rationalize the operation of the railways and pay a bridge subsidy for going around the lakes.
Once again there were high hopes that the railway systems would begin to operate more effectively and efficiently. In 1959 the MacPherson royal commission was set up with instructions to end once and for all this wasting of the nation s resources in the inefficient, uneconomic handling of our transportation system. As a result of the report of that commission under the leadership of Mr. MacPherson, this parliament debated in the House and in committee from 1964 to 1967 proposals to put into effect the main recommendations of the commission.
The hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac) mentioned that at that time there was a minority government and that all parties supported the legislation. That is true, Mr. Speaker. There was general recognition on the part of the government-which was Liberal-and on the part of the opposition parties that we finally had to put our house in order. As a rough estimate, I would think that 40 per cent of the total economy of this country is in large measure dependent upon the efficient operation of some mode of transportation. What did we do when we put that legislation throughh in 1966-67? We accepted the principles of the MacPherson royal commission report. They were two. The first principle was that we should encourage the railways and other forms of transportation to compete with each other-railways to compete with trucking, air transportation, pipelines, and so on, as well as sea and water transportation. There was a principle of compensatory payments that was accepted in principle at that time.
Second, we accepted the principle that has been historic for every parliament since 1967-that when in the national interest we had to do something to help a region, an area or a group

in the national interest, the taxpayers of Canada would pay for it and not require the payment to be made by the transportation carrier. Those two principles, of competition and compensatory payments, and the taxpayers willing to accept, for the national unity of the country, responsibility for anything we ask the carriers to do that was not economic, were accepted.
Almost 80 amendments were proposed during that debate. The government accepted most of them because there was a will among all parties to make the system work. All parties agreed, and decided that our transport system, involving new modes of transport and developments, was beyond the capacity of a single minister to handle-in fact, was beyond the capacity of two or three deputy ministers to handle: they did not have the time. The system is complex, vast, and all parties agreed that by putting so much responsibility on one minister who was busy with other duties and two or three deputy ministers, assisted by secretaries and engineers, we had made a mess of it. It was just too large for one small group to handle. To quote the words of the previous minister of finance, our transport system was "a mess".
Today I listened to the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), an urban member, speaking about the problems of urban transportation, about the problems of people who must use urban transit to enter and leave our cities. In my 20 years as a member of parliament I have seldom heard an urban member discuss transportation. Usually, when we discuss transportation, the urban members leave the House because, after all, it is only a matter for the rural people, the people of the prairies, the maritimes, the people of Quebec, of northern Ontario and the remote areas of British Columbia and the territories. On this significant-you might say-historical day an urban member spoke about the government's record on transit. I join the hon. member for York-Simcoe in hoping that other members representing cities-Vancouver, Montreal, Winnipeg, smaller cities like Calgary, Edmonton, Regina' Saskatoon, Halifax and others-will also speak in this debate.
Rising transportation costs are a main element in forcing up living costs and production costs, and high production costs make us less competitive with our world competitors. Transportation is still probably one of the most important responsibilities of any department of government. It is no accident, as I have said many times, that the largest committee room in the centre block is the railway committee room. For most of the last 100 years members of parliament have spent much time considering questions of transportation. All this has passed and we no longer use the railway committee room except for banquets and social occasions.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: And committees.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
This legislation will not give us the chance to use it again. I shall now deal with the principles at issue. The decisions we made during the last ten years were based on attempts to make our railways run their operations rationally. Surely no fair-minded person who
National Transportation Act
knows anything about transport techniques in the world will deny that Canadian National and the CPR-the two great national railways-and the PGE match in their operational techniques any railway in the world. Our railways are efficient. Compare them with the railways operating in the northeast United States. The railroads of our neighbours to the south are a mess. They are a catastrophe.
Consider the operation of the United States railway system which tries to haul tremendous tonnages of goods to southeast coast ports. It it were not for the Mississippi water system the transport system of the central United States would be a chaotic mess. We in Canada have fine, highly trained and dedicated working people doing a tremendous job on our railways. The failure of our railway system has been at the top level; the failure stems from management operating in Montreal and other cities, in offices remote from operations. You cannot learn transport problems if you are in a skyscraper. You must be out in the field, in the regions of the country, to learn about our transport problems.
Over the years people from all parts of this country have raised a litany of complaints about how the railways try to make money. Their lists of complaints would make a book as long as any you have read. Naturally, one tends to think of how the railways try to make money in one's own area because those examples come readily to mind. In my province of Saskatchewan we have a great tonnage of potash to move. One set of mines in my constituency produces close to three million tons of potash a year. But they could not get the railways to carry the potash. The railway said, "Oh, no. We are here for one purpose only, to carry wheat." So the government of Saskatchewan had to build a monstrous highway, superior to the Trans-Canada highway in quality, to allow trucks to haul that potash night and day to the American railway, the Great Northern, which took the potash to the great markets of the mid-west. Mr. Speaker, that kind of nonsense alienates the friends and supporters of our railway system.
Another example which gripes me has to do with the western portion of western Canada. In the early days, when we found oil and gas in that part of the country, we wasted much oil and gas-at least, we burned off all low pressure fuels. I went to one company which had a tremendous deposit of unused natural gas in the ground because they did not know what to do with all the surplus propane except flare it off, and I proposed to the company that they should go to the major railways and ask them to haul propane for an agreed charge. The company knew the propane was valuable and as good as natural gas, but they did not have the technology for shipping
I suggested they should haul the propane in big tanks covering the length of a couple of flat cars. I suggested they could service the prairies for 400 miles around and all Canada as far west as B.C., as well as markets in Montana and other parts of the United States. This fuel could heat our homes and run our cars and tractors. When the proposal was made to the railways, what did they say? Both of them said, in effect, Yes, we admit this business will be a money-maker for us, but

not in the first couple of years. We will not be ready for a couple of years, or not before you develop the market, for only then can we make money out of this traffic". Today the people of western Canada are bearing the heavy costs of pipelines built all over Alberta and Saskatchewan. Today one hears complaints about access to premium fuel for industry, fuel which should have been reserved for customers in the far distant regions of the country including Ontario and our American markets. The railways did this deliberately, 25 years ago not because they were against making money but because it was not their policy to take a loss for two years while markets were built up. I shall touch on this subject again when we consider the bill clause by clause.
More recently, the Hall commission travelled to the west. At every meeting farmers and businessmen rose and cited examples to show that the railways could carry more tonnage. The railways had applied to abandon thousands of miles of line, but under pressure-the commissioners being there-the railways admitted that they could make money in southeastern Saskatchewan. Farmers, using the railways' own figures, were able to prove that if the railways hauled grain east instead of west and then back east again, they would make more money. They were able to prove that right in that area there was a market which would be equivalent of many millions of bushels of wheat, but for another commodity, gravel. One gravel pit supplies gravel-short areas for 100 miles around. With the price the railways charge for hauling gravel, a lot higher than wheat but much lower than the truck haul, the railways could have knocked the trucks out of the gravel business and saved our roads. There would have been a tremendous increase in income. This short haul of 100 miles would have put all those lines into a black position on the economic ledger. The railways had no choice, under the presentation of those figures and the presentation of the commissioners, but to admit that all these lines in southeastern Saskatchewan should be kept. When we ended up that day with the royal commission, the general feeling was that instead of taking out some of our main lines we should add 40 miles of line to make it more efficient. I point out these examples to illustrate the fact that this type of representation has been made to royal commissions since the thirties. Just as long as royal commissions have recommended rationalization, just as steadily has the management of railways refused to accept it. In Saskatchewan we have railway lines running parallel for 100 miles, one CN and one CP. Why they cannot use one line for both trains I do not know. Every royal commission recommends it. I will come back to that matter.
In effect, Mr. Speaker, I have been trying to make a case for the fact that parliament has on several occasions spent a great deal of time trying to put legislation and principles on the statute books of this House that will direct our system into a more effective and efficient management of the whole transportation system, not just the railways. At the end of that debate ten years ago, one promise was made by the then minister on condition that we let the legislation go through.

The minister made a promise-which is on the record of this House-that no future abandonment of these reserve lines would be allowed until the railways showed their cost of operation. In spite of that promise by the then minister, the railways still have not provided to the people of Canada the cost of operating these lines.
The railways are a power unto themselves. Seven years ago some civil servants got permission from the government to convert Canada into the metric system. This group of civil servants told the grain companies, "This is going to be done. Do it." They told the oil companies, "This is going to be done. Do it". All those poor innocents thought that was the law and went ahead and prepared for it last February 1-but not the railways. They said that when they were good and ready they would convert. That is one issue. Parliament thought it had resolved that issue ten years ago. It has still to be resolved in this legislation. We have two commissions at the present time on this subject. The Snavely report is now before us. In plain, blunt terms, since the minister could not find any person in Canada who knew anything about railway costing-no one does, not even the railways-they went outside the country and got a man who came here to establish what it costs to haul grain.
Many members of this House have read the Snavely report. There is no evidence in there as to costing. There is simple and flat assertion that the railways say it costs this much, and another flat assertion from representatives of the grain companies that this is the estimate of the costs. All the royal commissioner did was to split the difference. They expect parliament, on that type of whistling in the wind or finding the wind with your thumb, to make a decision on what it costs to haul grain in western Canada.
Second, we have the Hall commission which deals with the rationalization of railways, the same thing we had in the three previous royal commissions. It also is to deal with rationalization of grain. That report is not in yet. Before we even try to discuss this bill intelligently we should have those two royal commission reports.
I want to move on to the main part of my remarks. 1 am going to differ from the hon. member for Battleford-Kinders-ley, the minister and the government, and put it into terms that every member of parliament will understand and, I hope, every person in this country will understand. In 1966-67, parliament-with the support of all parties-decided that the Minister of Transport, regardless of his politics, and the Department of Transport, were incompetent by their own track record to run this huge, vast, complicated, intermodal system of transportation in Canada. We, the members of parliament, decided to transfer the power of policy-making and regulation to a new board called the Canadian Transport Commission. That power was given ten years ago.
What does this bill do? It says, in effect, that the CTC is a mess, that it does not do the job parliament asked it to do. Therefore, we are going to change all the powers and policymaking from the CTC back to the minister, the department and the governor general in council. This bill centralizes the
March 3, 1977

power of over 40 per cent of this country into the hands of one minister, with his department, which has a track record of failure going back 40 years. It says we made the mistake of putting it into an independent, neutral board. If you look at the bill you will find they still repeat the principle of the MacPherson royal commission report that rates must be compensatory. There must be competition where possible. In the national interest, the national taxpayer will pay. There is no mention of the costing principle which is vital to the control of all types of transportation.
This bill moves all powers of transportation, representing about 40 per cent of the economic segment, over to the minister. The minister will now be known as the czar of all the railways, the czar of all the airlines, not only "Lang Airlines" but the whole bit. He will be the czar of all pipelines and the czar of all water carriers. We have a measure of this czar from watching what he has done over the past five or six years, ever since the LIFT program of 1970.
What we are doing in this bill is transferring power from an independent forum to a political forum-to the minister and to the cabinet. There is no mechanism here for control by parliament. We are simply going back to square one. It was a mess for 40 years, and we tried to get out of that mess by putting things into the hands of an independent body. Now we are going back to the old system.
I ask this question: "Does parliament, does this country, want this tremendous power we have turned over to the CTC-which never used it-turned back to the minister and to the deputy ministers enabling them to move at any moment, make announcements outside the House, push in programs or scrap them without anything being said in parliament?" Members have heard what happened to the promises made in 1974 with regard to urban transit assistance. In the maritimes they are being betrayed by the "at and east" rates. In addition, the minister has suggested that the Crowsnest agreement, going back many years, should be changed. This is what we are objecting to. This is what we are being asked to do. There is no limit to the minister's power except the governor in council. It will reside in a cabinet barely able at the present time to keep up with its duties. Yet ministers will now be expected to watch over an industry so vast and complex that parliament decided some years ago it was too big for any one department and that it should be placed in the hands of a 17-man commission.
I hope members of parliament who feel themselves responsible for the successful working out of this country's economic situation will think long and seriously before accepting such a situation. I should like to suggest to the minister that the unity of this country is more than a matter of politics. It is a matter of economics as well. In Saskatchewan we have just finished fighting a couple of by-elections. I know that the Liberals have been complaining that we were bringing federal issues into provincial affairs. But we cannot avoid federal issues in Saskatchewan because our province is so completely dependent upon the economic policies of the federal government.
National Transportation Act
We see our province, as well as others, being attacked by the federal government in areas which are ours under the constitution. We think of the petroleum administration bill, of the intervention of the government in the case between the government of Saskatchewan and one of its own companies which it was taxing. The federal government has been interfering in matters which were none of its business, including even the metric system. Why does this administration go out of its way to make changes without telling the people, without telling the provincial government? Does it think it can continue to do this without getting into trouble?
I realize it cannot be pleasant for the minister to sit in the House and have to listen to what I am saying, but he is the chief architect of the unpopularity of the central government of this country in the west. What he has done, as minister in charge of the Wheat Board, as minister of justice and as Minister of Transport, with all the powers he has, is something the west is not anxious to tolerate any longer. If the minister will accept in good faith that we on this side would like to see a better transportation system, let him please give us the benefit of the thought that there might be some ideas better than those presented in the bill before us.
The other day the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) made a speech in which he held forth as to the advantages of stability. He made it clear that the carriers and the captive shippers had to know what the policy was before the system could work properly-they had to make their plans, and so on.
I should like to turn to an even more fundamental criticism of this legislation, but before I do so I wish to suggest that the CTC never had a fair trial. We set up this 17-man commission. What did the government do? It put in charge of that commission two washed-out, beaten-up old politicians. They had run out of steam in the political arena and they took refuge in an organization whose decisions could affect 40 per cent of the economy of this country. They took over, all they did was study, study, study.
They never directed the railways to do anything, for the reason they had no power to direct. It was a case of the Department of Transport saying, "You should do this," and of the CTC saying, "We are studying the matter". There was a dichotomy. But surely the answer is not to put the system back into the hands of those who have proved they could not run it before. The answer, in my view, is to get at the cause of the problems in the CTC.
I have referred to the government's bad habit of putting politicians who need a rest home more quiet than the Senate in charge of powerful commissions and agencies. I suggest we should leave the CTC as it is but give the commission the power to direct the various carriers engaged in the transportation business. The old legislation of ten years ago merely said that the commission "may recommend". Knowing the history and attitude of railway management, I can say that any recommendation from a transport commission or similar body set up by parliament has about as much effect as a fly on an elephant's hide. This has been proven for 40 years. They are so

March 3, 1977
National Transportation Act
tough they do not even listen to the metric commission. The power has to be put into the legislation.
Tremendous efforts were made in speech after speech of mine ten years ago pleading with the government to give the CTC the power to direct. If that power were given, it would need to be accompanied by the power to enforce. Because we had accepted the principle of the national government paying for all the things the railways were asked to do in the national interest, we had the club in our hands. The minister at that time was Mr. Pickersgill. Members who read the answers he gave me over a series of weeks will see how they twist and turn. He said, in effect, "We are dealing here with private enterprise and we would not think of directing private enterprise to do something which was against its will". Then, when he ended up by appointing himself chairman of the board, it was obvious why he took the line he did. He did not want responsibility for directing anything.
Mr. Speaker, the power of direction and enforcement would give the CTC a chance to prove whether it can operate effectively or not. There is a second consideration, and it is dear to my heart. We have to give back to parliament control over the government of this country, and particularly over transportation.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
I said earlier, and I will mention it again, that the biggest committee room in this building is the railway committee room. I want to see that railway committee room filled again with members of parliament, backed up by the most skilled staff which money can buy and which knows the costing procedure, can question the railways, the bus companies and other transportation bodies as to cost, that knows what the law is and how to enforce it.
The CTC has been in place for ten years, but it still does not know the costing formulas of the railways. That is the reason we had to go to the country and get the Snavely report. Parliament must be given back its control. The system I proposed ten years ago was incorporated in a motion moved by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), and I seconded it. It was a very simple proposal. We used the example of the Commonwealth of Australia in suggesting that a statutory committee be set up. The statutory committee would not be dependent upon the whims of the prime minister and the cabinet. This committee of parliament would meet by statute with a chairman of the opposition and with a staff that was paid for by that committee and would be independent of the civil service and the carriers. This committee would watch the CTC, to see that it did not spend all of its time studying but directed and carried out the powers of parliament and laid down in the statute, and enforced government policies.
The question of costing was so embarrassing to Canada ten years ago that when the question of rates came up, one railway-the CPR-told the government that it lost money
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain).)
hauling grain in the year 1958; I think the loss was $17 million. This horrified the western grain companies in the prairie provinces and they collected an equal amount of money. They went down to New York, where the CPR had put forward its costing figures, and they hired an equally prestigious accounting group to look at the same figures. In due course they reported that the company had made money.
So you have one group of highly skilled accountants working for the CPR and saying that the CPR lost money. Another group of accountants working for the grain companies said the CPR had made money. What did the royal commission do? It hired an equally prestigious group of accountants to examine the same CPR figures, and they concluded that the railways either made money or lost money. I have their report here and all members should read it. They will never understand it because those who made it do not understand it.
I am simply pointing out, Mr. Speaker, that on this question of parliamentary control we must accept, in humility, that neither do we as parliamentarians have the time properly to control a CTC with such an involved, complicated and vast operation as they have to manage, but in that humility we have to accept that there is a need to hire people, if necessary at a cost of $200,000 or $300,000 a year, to give us the kind of competent advice needed to cope with the type of thing we are up against here in Canada where we do not know the costing of the railways. We do know more about the airlines and we know precisely the costing of pipelines because that matter is well in hand, but we do have to take on this question of railway costing.
I think that we in parliament would serve ourselves well if we were to provide, in this legislation, firstly that the CTC stayed with its present powers; secondly, that the CTC be given the power to direct and to enforce under the terms already outlined in the act; and, thirdly, that we in parliament should be the ones the watch the CTC, not the Minister of Transport. I would not care if he was the Lord himself; he would not have the time to look after this tremendously complex and vast operation.

I am afraid that the Liberal revolt is, frankly, a bit revolting. In terms of urban problems in the area of the lower mainland, we have heard a lot about the problems in Toronto. I have had an opportunity to travel in Toronto when the Union station was jammed full, but I will tell you that the transport facilities available to people in Toronto are vastly superior to the transport facilities available in the lower mainland of British Columbia.
It is time someone in the House took notice of the fact that the worst transit urban area in Canada is in the lower mainland of B.C. The reason for that is the crazy geography of the lower mainland. We have a long, narrow piece of land-a neck where people have to drive down a single corridor in order to get to work.
We have heard the promises made in 1974 about urban transportation.
