Mr. Speaker, I wish to make one or two comments about the motion presently before the House. I am interested in uranium production, refining and use in Canada and in the world. The refinery which is to be established in Saskatchewan of which the hon. member spoke will be the result of the policy adopted by the federal government in September, 1974. That policy proposed that the further upgrading of uranium and the "value added" process with respect to uranium produced in Canada should take place in this country, for in that way we could develop our uranium refining capacity in Canada and ensure that more jobs would stay in this country. At the time of the adoption of this policy, between 4,000 and 5,000 tons of uranium yellow cake were produced in this country.
The new uranium mine which came on-stream in Saskatchewan during the past year will lead to increased production, and the traditional producing areas of Beaver Lodge northern Saskatchewan, and Elliot Lake, Ontario, will also contribute to this increased production in Canada. I believe that by 1985 production in this country will amount to some 15,000 tons per year of yellow cake. The increased production of this mineral; will be tremendously valuable to Canada. Indeed, its value is escalating rapidly. Five or six years ago, uranium yellow cake sold at between $5 and $6 per pound. Today's spot prices are as high are as high as $40 a pound. Therefore, the further upgrading of our uranium to uranium hexafluoride or uranium oxide is important for our country.

I want to carry that argument a little bit further. I suggest that wherever possible uranium refineries should be located close by the areas where uranium is produced. For example, in Ontario our present refining capacity is located in southern Ontario. As we move to have additional uranium refineries constructed in the province, these should be located in northern Ontario where the principal mines are located. The secondary manufacturing processing jobs would then be located in the north.
Since 1969 we adopted a policy of regional development in Canada. It is designed to create more equality between the various areas of our country by having secondary manufacturing and processing plants locate in the slow growth areas of our country. We have provided incentives through the R.D.I.A. Act. If we have a policy where we take taxpayers' dollars to provide incentives to locate plants in designated areas of our country, we should carry it a step further and see that Crown corporations such as Eldorado locate their plants in the slow growth areas of Canada.
If we look at the plan being proposed for Ontario, we see that there exists an opportunity for this to be located on the north shore of Lake Fluron. It would provide 150 or 200 new jobs processing the resources of that part of Canada.
If we look at the unemployment levels in certain areas of the north shore of Lake Huron, we see that over $12 million has been paid as an average over the past four or five years in unemployment insurance benefits. We see large expenditures for the LIP and Canada Works programs. The LIP program has provided seasonal jobs during the winter months. Now with the Canada Works program it will cover other times of the year as well. There is a great advantage in seeing plants of this nature locate in northern Ontario where they would provide the jobs.
There is another aspect to the matter which bears consideration. If we locate uranium refineries close to areas where the productive capacity of the mines exist, we have an opportunity to dispose of the nuclear waste from the uranium refineries in the uranium disposal waste facilities that are there for uranium mines. That would seem to be a wise move rather than establishing new nuclear waste disposal sites at various locations throughout the country. Indeed, many people who have studied this problem believe that our nuclear waste should be put back into worked out uranium mines which is the ultimate place to dispose of nuclear waste.
Another aspect of locating uranium refineries in the general area of the producing mines is the public acceptance of this type of facility. In the north shore area, for example, practically every municipality has passed a resolution supporting the second uranium refinery for Ontario being located in the north shore area. Chambers of commerce in most communities in the area have supported the location of a refinery in that area, as well as many individuals and community groups. There is that public acceptance, understanding, and knowledge of the further processing of uranium in an area where there already is uranium production.
March 3, 1977

We should look at the sense of justice to the uranium producing areas which went through very severe economic crises during the sixties. Hon. members will recall that in the fifties there was great pressure to produce uranium for military purposes for the United States. During the sixties, the agreements which had been reached during the fifties for further options of production of uranium were cancelled.
Communities like Elliot Lake practically collapsed. They went from 20,000 or 25,000 people down to 5,000 or 6,000. The build-up from that to the present day situation, where there is a tremendous boom and expansion taking place, was long delayed because of the very uncertain future of uranium production during the sixties and early seventies. These communities have seen very difficult periods of time.
The situation now is very different. The ore bodies in areas like Algoma are worth dozens of billions of dollars with today's value of uranium. There is a strong feeling that areas like this should not only have the mining and plant jobs that occur with a uranium mining operation, but the secondary processing jobs should be located in those communities as well.
If we look at the uranium stock piling program of the sixties, we see that the uranium, most of which comes from Elliot Lake and is now stored by the government, has produced a profit of several hundreds of millions of dollars for the government.
If we look at the kinds of production of uranium ore that will take place during the next quarter century and the amount of tax dollars and royalties which will be realized by the federal and provincial governments, we see revenues flowing into federal and provincial coffers from this source ranking in the billions of dollars.
There is a very strong feeling that when uranium refineries are located in Ontario they should be located in the north. Thus not only would the mining jobs be realized, but also the jobs in secondary processing plants.
We realize that studies which have been carried out in Ontario, like those carried out in Saskatchewan, into the environment and economic feasibility play a factor. Indeed there would probably be an additional cost to locate a plant like this in northern Ontario. In addition to looking at the economic factors, I believe we should look at public acceptance and the possibility of the disposal of waste in the worked out uranium mines. These are compensating factors that should be recognized by the government and by Crown corporations such as Eldorado.
I hope these considerations will be taken into account by the government and by the Crown corporation when they locate plants like this, whether it be in northern Ontario where we have such a tremendous productive capacity for this mineral, or in Saskatchewan with its new discoveries in certain areas where it looks as though there will be significant production of uranium in the next quarter century.

We are dealing in this case with nuclear energy, a very dangerous field. I can understand why so many people are security minded about it. Thirty or 40 years ago, after the second world war, as developments in the atomic energy field were passing into civilian hands, there was a great deal of secrecy attached to it. The United States passed legislation imposing stringent secrecy with regard to the dissemination of certain information, and this attitude spilled over into Canada. But that was 35 or 40 years ago. We are now in a different era.
We have had experience, particularly in Ontario, of the serious consequences of the development of atomic energy. There is grave apprehension on the part of a great many people in Ontario and elsewhere because of developments in

March 3, 1977

Port Hope, Elliot Lake, and other places. 1 am sure that all kinds of assurances were given by the government and by the corporation at that time to the people living in the areas involved, just as I have no doubt that assurances will be given to the people of Saskatchewan. But in the light of what has happened, in the light of the serious concern felt by knowledgeable people in Canada and in other parts of the world, it is not good enough for us to accept bland assurances by government people, even by people as eminent as the parliamentary secretary, that everything is perfectly all right and that there is no need for us to be given the information for which we are asking.
I recall examining one government witness in connection with this question of the provision of information. He reacted with astonishment and alarm. He asked, "Why should you know what our experts know?"
My contention is that this information we are seeking today should be the property of the people. It relates, in particular, to those living in the area which is to be developed as a nuclear project. After all, it is their health, their lives, their property and their future which are at stake. Surely in these circumstances they should be privy to all decisions which are made, and the information should be available to them as long as it does not come within the category of being contrary to national security.
The parliamentary secretary says it is a commercial enterprise. There are indeed circumstances in which information which might give advantages to competitors of a corporation ought to be withheld. But this is not being cited as one of the grounds for withholding information in this case. I suggest as strongly as I can, because of what we know, that if there is any proprietary right at all here, that right is the property of the people of Canada. And the only way this right can be asserted is through the disclosure of the information.

Mr. Speaker, as I recall, this afternoon at five o'clock when I concluded my preliminary remarks we were actually looking at the bill itself, which is somewhat unique in this Chamber. From time to time I think it is useful for members to read what they are passing.
I want now to refer to proposed section 3(2) (d), which I will quote. It is the prime principle of this legislation which is now enshrined in the law that in the field of transportation
-competition within and between modes of transport should be encouraged where economic and technical factors permit;

March 3, 1977
National Transportation Act
That is the second major reason why this party cannot support the bill. What is outlined here is the enshrinement of the failure of the transportation policy of this and previous governments. It enshrines the kind of failure that we had right here in Ottawa when we put STOL aircraft to fly between this city and Montreal. That is the kind of competitiveness that is enshrined in the bill. If we continue to use that kind of philosophy in providing transportation in Canada, we will dig ourselves deeper and deeper into the mire. We will get into a hole which is even larger than the one we have now. When you go for the principle of competition between private carriers, what you will find is that the private carriers will take all the profitable parts of transportation, and the rest, us suckers, will carry the bill. That is what will happen to an even worse degree now. When you enshrine that principle, you eliminate the possibility of a cross-subsidy. Cross-subsidization means that with viable, efficient and profitable transport you eliminate the possibility of using the revenues to subsidize areas in the country which will never pay for themselves. They will never pay for themselves because that is not the kind of country in which we live. We do not have a situation like the situation in western Europe. Our country is almost unique in terms of transportation. The Soviet Union is one of the other countries in the world which faces the same kind of problems we have.

We talked this afternoon about who really pays for transport in this country. There is not a single system of transport which is not subsidized. Every time we walk on a sidewalk we should remember that the municipality subsidizes that sidewalk. The roads we drive on are subsidized. What really is amazing is that every time we take an aircraft our ticket pays only 31 per cent of the cost of that service. We are

not paying for the air traffic controllers, for the runways, or for the Mirabels across this country.
From this minister we have seen an elitist transportation policy. It is nice for us as members of parliament to fly back and forth across the country, but it is not much good for those who do not fly and, believe it or not, the vast majority of people of this country rarely, if ever, use an aircraft. If we could keep that in mind we could reverse these priorities a little bit, and we could see to it that ordinary people would have a proper and efficient means of transport. However, we will not have that as long as we enshrine these two principles into the law. One is the principle of competition between existing modes of transport, and the second is commercial viability.
Most people in this House have not had a chance, but we on the west coast have had a chance to examine the new policy the minister is introducing, the user pay concept. We have seen that in operation. We are the pilot project which the minister is using to demonstrate his user pay philosophy. The minister has accomplished some great things so far. I want to list some of the benefits the user pay concept has brought to British Columbia.
The minister has dismembered a viable company with ships which were specially constructed for the purpose of supplying isolated ports in British Columbia. That company could have operated with a profit had the minister simply followed the report of his own advisers. I refer to the Acres report, which suggested those ships could have been upgraded with further capital investment, and we would not have needed to subsidize that particular service. Instead, because of a rash and, I would say, ideological decision, or a decision which was without any flexibility at all, the minister destroyed a viable company.
This concept left 300 people working in that company without work. Some, however, did find work. Six jobs for these seamen were found in Halifax. That is the extent to which they have been able to re-employ the workers who lost their jobs as a result of the minister's destruction of Northland Navigation. I am glad to see the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Lee) in the House because most of the people who live in his riding are very interested in finding out what is going to happen.
Another thing the user pay concept has brought about is the loss of all the spin-offs as a result of the drying up of that water transportation business. I received a letter today from longshoremen in Prince Rupert who are now crying because they do not have enough cargo to keep them working. The port is being dried up to some extent. There has been a reduction in the amount of cargo which is being carried to that port, and not least of all is the disruption of normal communication to over 100 communities in the isolated parts of British Columbia.
What the minister has really done in a back-handed way has been to dump the entire passenger load and the entire traffic burden on the province of British Columbia. However, I am not going to get too excited about this because I think the minister has a rabbit in his hat, or something in his pocket. He

I certainly give the minister credit for trying to pull his own chestnuts out of the fire. He is always running around trying to solve problems he has created. It is a wonderful way to seem busy all the time. The minister creates a disaster and goes back, grabs a bucket of water, and tries to put out the fire. That is what he has been doing in British Columbia, and 1 hope for the sake of British Columbians that he has something for us. I hope he is able to produce something in the way of rational transportation, something different from sending the Prince Rupert into Bella Bella, letting the lifeboat over the side to try to load the passengers from Bella Bella. That was an excellent challenge to the people of Bella Bella. I thought they were not as amused as they should have been, and we were lucky we did not lose anyone over the side, but it worked. That is another one of those little pilot projects upon which the minister is working. He just drops those lifeboats over the side and gets everybody to row out.
1 would like to tell the minister that just because he is running the Lumba Lumba out of Prince Rupert does not mean we are in Tahiti. We actually need boats to move people out to those vessels. This really would be a laughable subject if it were not so serious to the people of British Columbia. This is a serious situation for isolated ports in British Columbia. Somebody should write a novel about what has happened to water transport in British Columbia.
We do know one thing, though, and that is that there are Liberal members of parliament from British Columbia who have been working very hard at this problem. Three of those members, the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) (Mrs. Campagnolo), the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson), and the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. Pearsall) were very proud to say that they were involved in the planning of this decision. The hon. member for Coast Chilcotin did not even use a lifeboat; he dived in right away. He did not fool around, and I must give him credit for getting off that sinking ship. Then there was the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport), who did not quite dive off the boat; she just stood on the burning deck and said, "My resignation is coming in six weeks if this ship burns". She is hanging in there and I think she has learned how to skate. Maybe it is the practice she had on the canal, but she has been skating very fast. She is making Guy Lafleur look foolish.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have an opportunity to participate in the debate today respecting Bill C-33. First of all I want to say that I support the bill. I have noticed the serious tone of the debate, and it is easy to understand why it would be serious when we consider that the total budget for the department for 1977-78 is well over $1 billion.
I wish to put forward some facts concerning these figures. For example, the number of Transport Canada employees, including the Canadian Transport Commission, is 21,629; Air Canada 20,600; Canadian National Railways, 82,256; and the approximate total for Crown corporations including the National Harbours Board, 108,000.
When we look at the tax dollars that form the total budget of Transport Canada, we can quickly come to the position of support for a bill which would give the minister more power to carry out his responsibilities.
In recent years there have been suggestions about a Canadian merchant navy that would put us in a better position to control the shipment of our natural resources, and there has been talk of action in regard to the Canadian railway debt similar to that recently announced for the St. Lawrence Seaway debt.
The figures will not only show but prove the importance of transportation policies and of planning together with general operations across the country. However, one cannot but wonder about the top-heavy bureaucracy found within the Department of Transport, with its many technocrats and bureaucrats. What chance of survival do these programs and policies have after they have gone through so many hands, and what one could term the watering down process?
I suggest that anyone familiar with Canadian transportation history will say that this is an excellent time to review possible
[Mr. Leggall.)
changes and to consider changing the structure and hierarchy of the Department of Transport. Therefore, logically, we ought to establish a superministry of transport, under which would come two junior ministries with responsibility for implementing our transport policy. Certainly the present job is too onerous for one man. I suggest that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) cannot at the same time oversee the day-to-day operations of the ministry of transport, the CNR and Air Canada while carrying out his additional responsibilities for the Canadian Wheat Board.

I have thought of some new titles. For instance, deputy ministers could be known as chief administrators, or chiefs of Staff, and parliamentary secretaries as deputy ministers reporting directly to the House. For too long we have heard references about various departments of the federal government working at cross-purposes. This has been counterproductive and created, indeed compounded, some of our present problems.
While considering amendments to the act I suggest that we should look closely at how efficiently the large numbers of employees presently employed by MOT do their work. I sometimes feel that if they are not compelled to work efficiently and productively they could well fall into the category of the invisible unemployed.
I now mention transport subsidies, specifically in the Atlantic region, and wish to put some facts and figures on record. Three major transport subsidy payments, covering five areas, transferred approximately $280 million to the Atlantic region in 1976. These payments can be broken down as follows: for rail passenger subsidy, $35 million; ferry and coastal services, $100 million; west bound freight subsidies, to rail $8 million, and to truck $3.5 million; west bound selective freight, to rail $2 million, and to truck $1.5 million; intra-provincial freight subsidy, to rail $10 million, and to truck $20 million. Where will all this money go when the proposed changes regarding these subsidies are implemented? Keep in mind that in excess of $1 billion has already been allotted to the Department of Transport budget. Therefore it should be obvious that only a small percentage of the department's total expenditures have application to the Atlantic provinces.
Considering recent decisions concerning subsidies, and previous speakers spoke about subsidies to east and west coast ferries, it is clear that we must let the public understand the philosophy which will lead to a change in subsidy policy in Canada. We have already seen evidence of the workings of this philosophy on both the east and west coasts. One cannot cut
March 3, 1977

subsidies without negotiating and consulting with those who entered into original agreements in good faith. Agreements have been reached with certain provinces. I say that we must be cautious in our attempts to reduce subsidies in various provinces. Surely one will not argue that the matter of reducing assistance with respect to the Crowsnest Pass ought to have been addressed some 20 years ago. Why not commence negotiations to bring that particular agreement into line with modern day needs? If an agency which requires 30 per cent assistance receives a subsidy of 70 per cent, I am sure the Canadian people would want that particular subsidy to be discussed, negotiated, and adjusted.
We must be cautious not to forget our direct responsibilities. I say this because subsidy payments in the estimates submitted this morning by the Minister of Transport accounted for more than half the 1977-78 budget of the department, or more than $500 million.
When the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications visited the west coast last year it saw the harbour facilities at Vancouver, and visited Seattle, U.S.A. We quickly saw that equipment at Vancouver needed modernization. I am speaking both of dry dock facilities and over-the-side equipment for loading goods and grain. Obviously, we shall need to do something to remain competitive. We must upgrade our facilities to maintain our excellent reputation and induce ships to use our ports on the west coast, as well as those on the east coast. We shall need to spend money on additional equipment, and on upgrading existing facilities at Halifax and Saint John, New Brunswick, as well.
I now turn to the matter of debt. The CN debt has already been mentioned, and we know Air Canada incurred a $25 million deficit last year. This morning, when the committee was considering the 1977-78 estimates, I addressed a question to the Minister of Transport. I know that steps will be taken, under spending policies to be implemented, to curb, if not eliminate, that deficit.
Talking of Air Canada brings me to the problems confronting Eastern Provincial Airways serving Atlantic Canada, and the airline's application before the Canadian Transport Commission last year. I cannot participate in this debate without, in all justice, stating the case of the citizens of Atlantic Canada. The chairman of the air branch of the commission brought down a most unsatisfactory decision. He is a westerner and visited the Maritimes more than once to conduct hearings.
Consider the effort that goes into the presentations that are made to the air branch of the Canadian Transport Commission. Many long hours and a lot of money go into their preparation. What is the result? Last December the decision was handed down by the chairman of the committee. He did not give a positive consideration to the applications placed before the CTC. The applicants were willing, ready and able to implement the program of transportation for which they were seeking the class two licence. In its wisdom, the CTC air
National Transportation Act
branch decided to give it to a firm which had encountered financial difficulties three months prior to the decision being handed down.
Decisions of this type encourage me to speak in favour of the amendments contained in Bill C-33. The bill recommends that some of the decision making process be taken out of the hands of the CTC and more of this power given to the Minister of Transport.
I witnessed the disppointment and frustration as the result of the negative approach taken by the air branch of the CTC with regard to giving positive consideration to the plight of the citizens of Atlantic Canada. It almost brings one to look for the resignation of, if not the whole board, at least the chairman.
Consider the expenditure involved in conducting these hearings. Think of the time, effort and investment, both financial and sweat equity, that are contributed to these hearings. With a negative response like that, we wonder whether it is worth wasting our time following that type of procedure.
In central Canada there is talk of improving the Windsor corridor. We hear about better transportation for Ottawa, Toronto, Montreal, Quebec and Vancouver. However, in 1977 there is no modern air passenger service linking the four Atlantic provinces.
I live in northern New Brunswick. In order to travel to Halifax, I have to get on a train at six o'clock in the morning. Twelve hours later I arrive in Halifax. No modern air facilities are available. In order to get to the capital of the province of New Brunswick I have to spend six hours on roads that are exactly not up to trans-Canada specifications.
