speechtext: Speak to the provincial government.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
If I understand the news correctly, they have problems other than highways at the moment. However, that is not what I wanted to speak about.
There has been positive input by DREE and the Department of Transport to try to eradicate that kind of situation. There was a recent announcement of $42 million to match the $10 million or $11 million being put in by the province to continue improving the highway network between Moncton and Camp-bellton, New Brunswick, Route 11. Another $5.5 million will be spent on Route 17. There is no question as to the urgency, considering how many years the trans-Canada has been completed from Newfoundland to British Columbia.
It is about time the provincial government accepted its responsibility to complete that important link which brings us to la Belle Province and the Gaspe area, not only for economic reasons and the whole question of regional development but the very matter of tourism.
To come back to the negative decision by the Canadian Transport Commission, the applicant that had the technical wherewithal to implement that service did not receive a favourable hearing. E.P.A. Ltd. could not get approval for a class two licence. E.P.A. Ltd. recently cancelled its order with the de Havilland Corporation at Downsview for a Dash-7. This

March 3, 1977
National Transportation Act
50 passenger aircraft would have been used to link the four Atlantic provinces. It is the obvious answer to a most serious problem.
From conversation with the Council of Maritime Premiers and other elected representatives, I know they have not given up on this. In fact they are now working in earnest. If that is the attitude of those who sit on the board and conduct the hearings, we will have to set our sails and cut the cloth accordingly.
I am convinced there will be complete co-operation and support from all elected representatives from that area for a new approach. In the very near future a new application will be made to the Ministry of Transport for a more favourable consideration with regard to the approval of funds in order that we in the maritimes might have modern air facilities. We would like to enjoy the same facilities as the rest of Canadians.
I support the view that was expressed previously with regard to the top heaviness of various departments. A good example is in the Department of Transport and the Crown corporations such CN and Air Canada.
There should be a better system for input by members of this House. Much debate could go on as to what the format should be. I stated previously that we should look seriously at stripping some of the powers away from the too powerful bureaucrats such as deputy ministers who sometimes get carried away with their ivory tower building. They forget the human side, the needs and aspirations of Canadians on many different fronts.
One solution with regard to the day to day operations of corporations such as CN and Air Canada might be to have more input by politicians at some level, whether they sit directly on the board or act as advisers. I am not looking for more structure. We have enough of that now. However, it is time to bring some of the decision making process to where it should be, with the elected representatives.
There is no question but that our transportation system, rail and air, is one of the best operated compared with other countries. Notwithstanding the problems of wrestling with the media, the present minister is very dedicated and hard working. He has to tolerate jabs and babblings in our day-to-day deliberations and debate in this House. I am sure all serious Canadians will agree with me when I say this minister has dedicated his energy 100 per cent in an effort to come to grips with the problems which face us. The importance of the transportation sector and the proportion of Canadian tax dollars which it consumes make it evident that the time has come not only to support the amendments in Bill C-33 but to support the minister in a more positive way so that in the implementation of these policies he can bring about even better solutions.
We have heard presentations by members in all quarters of the House, both in this Chamber and in committees, in favour of the establishment of a Canadian merchant marine. While no provision is made for this in the estimates, this is a

possibility we ought seriously to consider especially in the light of such developments as the export of increasing quantities of coal to Japan. There is no reason why we should not place ourselves in the position of exercising better control over the distribution of our national resources.
I conclude, as I began, by saying I will support the amendments contained in Bill C-33.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this bill I must say at the outset that I was more than a little surprised that the minister himself did not choose to present the first major revision of the National Transportation Act since its passage almost ten years ago. Though he has not addressed the House on this bill, I trust he has read the speech which was delivered by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) on his behalf, and that at least he approved it. It would be fair, I suggest, to hold him in some way accountable for what was said by the Minister of Justice when he introduced this measure.
In a way, the absence of the minister was ironic. The minister chose not to be present, but on the other hand he is asking for great power to be restored to the Department of Transport with respect to the day-to-day workings of the transportation system. Under the new legislation, policies could be changed at will and transportation programs could be made to operate to the great benefit of certain regions or, conversely to their detriment. As I say, I find it passing strange that the minister should have chosen not to be present on this occasion, and I see that my feelings are shared by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner).
Nevertheless, we are grateful that the hon. gentleman, among all the ministers who have presided over the National Transportation Act, has been the most frank. He alone has been prepared to say what none of his predecessors dared say, that is, that the legislation enacted by Mr. Pickersgill was an attempt to put the transportation system on a footing completely different from that of a policy based on consideration for the social and economic well-being of the country as a whole. It is clear in retrospect-and later I should like to quote a passage from the remarks of the Minister of Justice, one which no doubt reflects the minister's own views-that the fundamental shift which took place as a result of the Mac-Pherson Royal Commission and later the Transportation Act, was to enunciate that a first priority would be to make a transportation system in this country commercially viable and that in a sense every other aspect of transportation policy would have to be subservient to that basic goal and commitment.
I suppose that anyone who looks at this concept superficially would say it makes a great deal of sense-surely a transportation system should be commercially viable and efficient to the extent possible. The only difficulty is that when we make this the main raison d'etre of a transportation policy we begin to fly in the face of the economic, social, and political history of this country. A number of speakers in the debate have referred to this aspect and to the damage which the act and its administration have done to the several regions. Indeed, it was
March 3, 1977

the minister's own surrogate, the Minister of Justice, who said, on Tuesday, I think it was-and I quote from page 3526 of Hansard-referring to the probable national implications of various direct and indirect freight subsidies:
Most of these were implemented when the economic and transportation needs of the West, Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces were significantly different from what they will be in the coming decades. Some of these programs, however well-intentioned and effective years ago, now actually inhibit the development of certain regions and parts of the transportation system. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport has proposed changes in a number of these assistance programs.
Those of us who come from the more distant regions of the country should be grateful for two things. First, for recognition that the actual impact of the transportation policy has for the last decade been one of "user pay". That has been the reality of the present transport policy. The second is because the minister has recognized that the policies which have been in place affecting a great many of these regions have been inappropriate and must be changed.
I suppose the minister was bound to get the message eventually. Certainly it was delivered to him from a number of different quarters. Almost a year ago the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) tabled a report in which he analyzed various sectors within his jurisdiction. With respect to transportation in Prince Edward Island he said in a document tabled before the standing committee last spring:
The report stated that the problems involved in transporting commodities using existing facilities are expected to be extreme by 1977.
That opinion was fortified by further comments made by provincial ministers in the legislature of Prince Edward Island during the spring session of a year ago.
When I asked the minister on March 26 of last year what steps were being taken to head off this impending crisis, he replied, in the way he so often does:
We always try to analyze traffic trends and look ahead to the steps to be taken to accomodate them, and that is what we are doing.
That kind of bland assurance does not convince us that the minister recognized the seriousness of the situation. It did not take too long for the provincial governments of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and New Brunswick to come back with a much sharper review and to remind the minister, if there is any danger of his forgetting, that there were serious problems respecting transportation policy in the region and that there seemed to be no awareness of this on his part, or on the part of the federal government generally.
At the twenty-second meeting of the Council of Maritime Premiers, which took place shortly after that in Charlottetown, the maritime premiers went on record as saying, first of all, that they would request an early meeting with the federal Minister of Transport. The premiers reaffirmed their position that transportation systems should be used by governments as positive tools for the attainment of national and regional objectives. But they stated that, despite the federal government's agreement with their position, there was an alarming lack of hard evidence that transportation is in fact being used
National Transportation Act
as a positive development tool. Indeed, they said there were examples of just the opposite. They went on to say:
The premiers expressed concern that the federal government is increasing cost recovery within some transportation systems without considering the effects of this on the over-all economy.
Finally the Minister of Transport in his generosity agreed to meet last summer with the maritime premiers to consider their particular plight. I would like very much to have the tapes of that particular meeting because I understand that it was a very stormy and long affair. However, at that point at least, it did not provide any evidence of change on the part of the Minister of Transport with respect to his various policies.
It took considerably more time before the minister finally responded. The response, as hon. members know, came just a few days ago at the meeting which took place in Charlottetown, where he met with the three provincial premiers and the minister of transport for Newfoundland. I am going to say something about the results of that meeting in a few minutes, Mr. Speaker, but I merely rehearse these facts to indicate what a dreadfully long time it took, and what a difficult task it was, to convince this government that it indeed had some responsibility with respect to the regional impact of national transportation policies.
The danger I see in general terms in the position that the minister has had advanced on his behalf by the Minister of Justice, and indeed by the nature of agreements that seem to have been arrived at, is that in some way the minister is prepared to rationalize the Canadian transportation system as some kind of cost accounting method of bringing down certain expenditures within the Department of Transport, and in very real terms will lock in the status quo.
The tip of the hat that the minister has now given in the context of his meeting with the Atlantic premiers recognizes that the factor of regional, economic and social need will play a part. But beyond that general statement, which is stated quite often in the speech that was made on Tuesday, there is no real definition regarding what major change of policy will take place. Indeed we were told as a result of that meeting that there will be specific amendments made to the transportation act, which in itself is an amendment before the House; but so far the minister has not seen fit to present these amendments. He was not here to introduce his bill, and he has not yet said what form these amendments will take. We are merely told that some consultations are going on with Atlantic governments and that at some point after second reading, presumably in committee, the minister will bring forth some amendments to this bill.
I think that that kind of general but non-commital indication is insufficient to guarantee to the regions of this country that the government has satisfactorily learned of the disadvantage and disparity that it has created through the operation of this transportation policy over the last decade. Surely until we get some firm indication of the exact details of these transportation amendments, it would be a foolish thing for any member, from the government or from the opposition, to give his blank cheque for the speedy passage of this legislation.

March 3, 1977
National Transportation Act
Much of our attention in the context of this debate focuses quite naturally on the railroad. It was, after all, the building of the railroad itself which, in a sense, drew together the fragments of this country into one nation. As the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) mentioned a little earlier, even portions of that have not yet been completed. We are seeing the sorry spectacle in some instances of railroads not being completed and rail lines being abandoned.
Those of us from Atlantic Canada, particularly from the provinces of Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island, are less than enthusiastic about the way in which the Canadian National Railways have defaulted in their responsibility to contribute to the economic well-being of these two provinces. Surely the basis for British Columbia and the maritime provinces joining Confederation was that of establishing some firm rail connections to link the country together. Indeed the very history of Prince Edward Island's entrance into Confederation was the sorry spectacle of a railroad that wandered everywhere but in the right direction. Having exhausted the financial capacity of the territory, as it was then, it was forced through bankruptcy to enter Confederation.
The railroad, like fiscal arrangements, is mentioned in the British North America Act, a sign of its importance in the eyes of maritime governments. With respect to the particular history concerning freight rates, which has been a continuing burden for the Atlantic provinces, it is important for members to have recalled to them briefly how we have arrived at the situation where today rail transportation has put an enormous burden on the backs of those people in Atlantic Canada.
The Maritime Freight Rates Act, which was passed by parliament in the early months of 1927, was a direct result of the Royal Commission on Maritime Claims, very often referred to as the Duncan commission. This commission was appointed in 1926. It attempted to study what had happened with respect to freight costs, particularly between the time 1912 to 1925. It discovered in fact that, using statistics supplied by the railways, between 1912 and 1925 there was a 92 per cent increase in rates, while elsewhere in Canada they had increased in the same period by only 55 per cent. It would seem that this royal commission was able to uncover the very great burden that was disproportionately placed during that period on the people of Atlantic Canada. I quote two brief sections that appear on page 21 of the report of that royal commission:
The lower level of rates that prevailed on the Intercolonial Railway system prior to 1912 is, in our view, rightly to be interpreted as the fulfilment by successive governments of the policy and pledges that surrounded the railway from its inception.
There was a policy, particularly when the railroad was very largely controlled in the region, to use transportation as a development tool, so that during that period local industry and other opportunities could be developed to their full.

Then the Duncan commission went on to state:
On the broader question, however, of the incidence of the existing rales as a whole upon industry and employment in the Maritimcs, we have come very definitely to the conclusion that the rate structure as it has been altered since 1912 has placed upon the trade and commerce of the Maritime Provinces (a) a burden which, as we have read the pronouncements and obligations undertaken at Confederation, it was never intended it should bear, and (b) a burden which is, in fact, responsible in very considerable measure for depressing abnormally in the Maritimcs today business and enterprise which had originated and developed before 1912 on the basis and faith of the rate structure as it then stood.
I think that, therefore, this kind of disproportionate increase is to recognize one of the sad facts that has been all too frequent since Confederation. Transportation, rather than being used as a tool of development, even though that was its basic concept at the time of Confederation, has been used to the disadvantage of the region, but perhaps nowhere more deliberately or more frequently has this occurred than since the enunciation of the National Transportation Act about a decade ago.
I should like to quote from a question of my colleague, the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), on July 12, 1975, as reported at page 7813 of Hansard. He was comparing here the situation in terms of rate increases on the St. Lawrence Seaway as against rail rates in Atlantic Canada. He asked:
How many times has the government raised rates on the St. Lawrence Seaway system since 1959?
The answer was:
The St. Lawrence Seaway Authority advised as follows: I. There have been no increases in the Montreal-Lakc Ontario section of the seaway. Tolls on the Welland canal were suspended in 1962. A lockage fee, phased in over five years, was introduced on this canal in 1967.
The second question was:
How many times were rail rates from Atlantic Canada inland raised since 1959?
The answer was:
The Canadian Transport Commission advises as follows: 2. During the period January I, 1959 to June 11, 1975 inclusive, rail rates from Atlantic Canada inland were raised as follows; under categories indicated: (a) normal class and commodity rates, eight times, (b) Truck and water competitive rates eleven times, (c) Agreed charges, six times.
Since that question was tabled a little over a year and a half ago there have been at least four more freight increases. The sad fact is that there has been an acceleration in increases, particularly since the late 1960's. Under the Maritime Freight Rate Act, which was in existence prior to that time, there was a ceiling with respect to these increases, but the exorbitant and unwarranted increases that have occurred since the late 1960's have increasingly placed Atlantic Canada at a competitive disadvantage. It is for that reason, if for no other, that there is adequate need for us to have a revision, not only of the National Transportation Act, which is certainly long overdue, but of the policies and programs that will go with it.
I think it is obvious that the outcry of the Maritime premiers last year, and the comments of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard), give an indica-

March 3, 1977
tion of the general anxiety and the general awareness that there is need of concrete action on the part of the minister, the department and the government.
What I am concerned about is that the minister act on the verbal commitments that were given to the maritime premiers and to the Newfoundland minister of transport. There are some specifics. Certainly the situation in Prince Edward Island with respect to commodity transport is becoming extremely serious. Not only I but my colleagues on the other side of the House have tried to bring this to the attention of both the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) with respect to the transportation of our basic commodity, that is, potatoes. But there seems to be a very indolent or half-hearted attitude concerning the carriers that will be used to move these potatoes to market.
There has been little or no recognition of the fact that we have seen a very rapid decline both in number and in quality of the reefers that have been used to move potatoes to market. Less than a decade ago we had well in excess of 4,000 of these cars; four or five years ago we were down to 2,500. It was originally expected that we might be down to about 1,500 this year, but the figure is much closer to 1,000.
As the minister would know if he contacted authorities in the potato industry in P.E.I. and New Brunswick, there are reports of increasing shortages this season. There are difficulties in organizing shipments of potatoes either to port or to export markets or to central Canadian markets, and yet the minister tells us that studies are going on, that there has not yet been a decision as to whether or not the new intermodal use, the use of trailers that will be driven to central points and loaded by piggyback on the train and taken to central Canadian markets, will replace the present use of rail cars. Yet I have not met one single individual, either in the potato industry or working with CNR, who believes to any degree that for many years to come we will not need a substantial number of rail cars to move well over two-thirds or three-quarters of our crop to market.
For a whole variety of reasons, both in terms of terminal points and in terms of having sufficient carriers available at reasonable cost, and in terms of organizing shipments that can get to market in this fashion, it will not be possible for five, ten, or 15 years to move more than a small percentage, perhaps no more than 15 per cent or 20 per cent at maximum by the intermodal system. In the foreseeable future we will depend on the railroad to move potatoes to the market. Yet the minister is reluctant even to place an order for 500, 700, or 800 reefer cars to tide us over this serious sitution. He said that more study must go on, more consultation. This week his colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, told us that he is not sure the producers will actually use these cars. He is certainly not basing that on any direct conversation he has had with anyone in the potato industry. Quite likely he is basing it on some reports from the CNR and on some cars that stood idle early in the season when everything was moving directly by ship to European markets.
National Transportation Act
It is about time the minister got together with some of his colleagues. It is about time he took action, or the kind of extreme situation that was forecast by his colleague, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, a year ago will come to fruition. It will not make me or any other member of the House happy to be able to say, "We told you so". That will not help the poor potato grower who will be stuck with a product which he will in no way be able to get to market. It is obvious that a decision will have to be taken with respect to this commodity.
The only question is how soon the minister will move, and whether he will move soon enough to head off a crisis which could well arise. The minister has been willing in the past to order some thousands of grain cars to service a market which he knows exists and requires this service primarily in western Canada. It is unexplainable to the people in my area why that same kind of response cannot occur with respect to the situation in P.E.I. and New Brunswick. I understand it could well be important because of a different delivery system for some of the horticultural producers in western Canada.
There are other questions. I do not want to spend all my time on this issue even though it is of basic concern to me as a representative from the potato growing area. I hope that the minister and his officials will take this additional plea very seriously.
I do want to deal, however, with the more general issue with respect to the minister's commitment about taking regional needs, objectives, and ends much more seriously. It seems to me there are a number of unanswered questions, questions which I think must be looked at very squarely. When the minister or his colleague, the Minister of Justice, said that basic consideration will be given or, to be more accurate, when he said that the policy basically implies that whenever national or regional, economic or social ends do not justify a transportation subsidy then the user of the facility or service should pay, what did he mean by national or regional, economic or social ends? There have been no indications since the meeting which the minister had with the Atlantic premiers back in the early part of February that he has a definite concept in mind of what kind of agreements he wanted to reach. What criteria will exist, so that everyone will know that this policy will be administered according to those particular ends and objectives?
Perhaps more important than the criteria-though certainly the criteria are a fundamental consideration-the second question is, who will make the determination? We are told that there is going to be much more consultation and co-operation. I am sure there are many people with a direct interest in the transportation industry who will be delighted to hear that the minister has discovered that transportation is something about which there has to be very close consultation and co-operation. But with whom will there be this consultation and co-operation? I suppose it will be with the provincial governments, with agencies, Crown corporations and others involved in the trans-

March 3, 1977
National Transportation Act
portation field, but does it also mean other federal departments? Will it also be with respect to the development of employment opportunities under the Department of Manpower and Immigration, or with respect to commitments to develop new industry under DREE, or a change in tariff policy under the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, or with respect to the improvement or expansion of agriculture so that these will be factors bearing on the situation concerning regional, economic or social ends? We are not told. We have not heard. The minister has remained silent, both inside and outside this House.
We have a press release which the minister kindly circulated, but that gives little information or clarity to the responsibilities the minister or his department will exercise in this regard. Perhaps more important even than the question of criteria or who makes the determination is the basic dollar and cents question as to what funds we are talking about. Indeed it is in the area of funding that I am beginning to wonder whether the minister has really made any commitment at all because at one point in his release, which is also carried in the press communique from the twenty-fifth session of the Council of Maritime Premiers, the minister says, and I quote:
Mr. Lang indicated his acceptance of the general principle that the federal government would re-allocate funds, resulting from a reduction in subsidy payments, to other essential priority transportation projects and programs in the region.
What a beautiful phrase, but how little it tells us of what funds, and to what extent these funds will be used to make transportation a positive tool for development in the regions of economic and social disparity in this country. Without some clear commitment as to the amount of funds we are talking about, more than vague terms such as re-allocation and re-orientation, we have very little to make us believe that there will be any substantial improvement or closing of the gap with respect to disastrous transportation policies and costs which have been in effect over the past decade.
Then, I suppose, most of all we have to be clear as to how this transportation policy with respect to regional objectives and ends is going to be administered and how it is going to be implemented. There are a whole series of questions which I would love to have the time to put on the record arising out of one report which was produced a little less than a year ago by the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission. They made a number of pungent observations, and raised a number of questions which surely need to be answered in the context of the agreement the minister appears to have arrived at with the four Atlantic governments.
I am going to quote two or three questions. The report notes on page 9 that rail freight traffic originating in the Atlantic provinces is in decline. What are the longer term implications for the region of this decline? Are there any viable methods by which the existing rail network could be more vigorously used to assist the region, or is it not worth the effort and the expense?
With respect to the over-all freight rate increase for rail of 85 per cent to 90 per cent last year, how serious is this for an

Atlantic producer competing in the Ontario market? Were the various rate increases spread out fairly evenly across the country, or did they favour certain regions and industries more than others? What would be the effect of giving the provinces more jurisdiction over rates within their borders?
As I say, those connected with transportation within the region have a number of basic questions which need to be answered, but it seems to me that perhaps the most fundamental question of all is the question which has not yet been answered by the minister either in his press communique or, 1 doubt, in his meeting with the Atlantic premiers, or in any other place of which 1 am aware, and that question is, how does he view the long-term development of this country?
Does the minister believe that in administering the proposed transportation legislation he has some duty and some responsibility to play an activist role with respect to the chronic economic and social disparity which has existed in certain regions of the country for too long? Does he believe, when he looks at the income situation in certain communities in areas in parts of Newfoundland, Cape Breton, Prince Edward Island, or in eastern Quebec, which reflect an income of half the level of the national average of this country, that transportation is involved in that question? When he looks at the recent figures indicating that half the people who are unemployed come from east of the St. Lawrence River-roughly half a million people-does he believe that transportation is critically involved in solving that unacceptable human tragedy? What are the over-all goals of a new transportation act? That is perhaps where we should end this little talk this evening in looking at the National Transportation Act itself.
When one looks at the goals and the objectives set out in this bill, it is no wonder that the four governments of the Atlantic provinces unanimously agreed that, right at the outset, both in terms of the preamble and the objectives of this bill, there is not a clear recognition that transportation should be used as a tool for the economic and social health of the regions of this country. It is true that in one clause we read:
It is hereby declared that the objective of the transportation policy for Canada is to achieve a transportation system that
(a)	is efficient,
(b)	is an effective instrument of support for the achievement of national and
regional social and economic objectives . ..
I understand that by changing that and a couple of other clauses, there may be some further recognition of responsibility, but from my point of view, and perhaps from the point of view of very many people, unless the minister can clearly state at the outset that this bill is seen in the context of transportation as serving the reduction of regional disparities and the elimination of long-standing transportation inequities which exist in this country, we will not feel we have benefited from the amendments the minister placed before us this week. Quite frankly, for a Minister of Transport not to realize that, is surely to miss the essential point of this country. Surely there are two things which stand out for someone who looks at this just for a moment. I think we are the second largest country in the world and yet we have a population which is so small,
March 3, 1977

relatively speaking. But it is so strung out that our great problem on a day-to-day basis is remaining viable as a country.
There has been a tremendous amount of attention paid to the situation vis-a-vis the future of Quebec and its relationship to the rest of the country, but surely germane to that situation and to all the provinces and regions of the country is the fact that unless something as basic as transportation works day by day in a whole series of ways to relieve the difficulties and the disadvantages which exist for a person who is a consumer in Charlottetown or a potato grower in part of my riding, it is not serving the nation well as a whole. Frankly, 1 have been disturbed that the Minister of Transport has taken so long even to begin to recognize that situation. Even in response to the questions that 1 and others have raised with him about the concept of user-pay, he having recognized it was no longer valid, and whether he would state clearly and unequivocally that from this time forth transportation policies would be used as a positive tool for development and, if you like, national equalization, as a positive tool to open up communities that have existed far too long at the end of transportation links that have done them a disservice-and whether this will be overcome with avengeance-that is not what I hear from the Minister of Transport. I hear that if it is appropriate, and if the objective is warranted, there will be relocation and reorientation.
At another point we are told that the minister and the maritime premiers agreed that, where economic development objectives required it, these objectives would take precedence over the commercial viabilities of the services concerned, and that later on they agreed on the merits of applying the subsidy only to selected commodities and only to shippers of regionally produced commodities. Even there, there is no recognition of the inbound situation. There was some grudging admission that perhaps we should do something for producers in places like the Atlantic region with respect to central Canadian markets. That is only half the equation; there is still the importing of raw materials and equipment in order to begin to be productive and competitive with the rest of the country.
To date we have heard no explanations, no assurances, no call to establish a transportation policy that is really going to reduce and redress regional imbalances and inequities. Without that assurance we do not have a real transportation policy, but a hollow mockery of one.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in engaging in this debate on major transportation policy I should like to discuss a number of issues of particular interest to me, and I would gather them under five separate headings.
The First is one which I know other members from urban areas have already spoken about. It relates to the pressing need for federal aid to urban transit.
National Transportation Act
The second issue 1 should like to speak about, perhaps a little more philosophically, and to put forward ideas on that 1 think are important, relates to inter-urban transport.
The third matter I should like to touch upon is what 1 consider a very important subject relating to the safety factor at open level crossings. 1 refer more specifically to major urban areas where this is a continuing and serious problem.
The fourth matter I should like to address myself to is the construction of grade separations, which has some direct reference to the earlier topic, but still is a topic on its own because of the vast sums of money that will ultimately be needed.
The last topic is the role of the Canadian Transport Commission in some of the areas of its responsibility, particularly its role as I see it as a responsible public forum in the service of the people of Canada.
On the matter of aid to urban transit, I think this is indeed a most important area in which governments should and must become involved, including the federal government. In coming to this general conclusion I think one only needs to pose the question of what kinds of areas should government be involved in, in the First place, and specifically the federal government. It seems to me that the answer is government at the federal level should be involved where there is a need felt by a large number of citizens, where there are social injustices, of one kind or another, and the demand, for whatever reason, is there.
In cities like Montreal and Toronto we have some 20 per cent of the Canadian population. I do not have exact figures but I would guess that probably 40 per cent of the population in those two cities is moving about every day from home to job and back-not in inter-urban transportation, not flying from city to city or travelling by train from city to city, but getting up in the morning and going to work, not travelling for pleasure or enjoyment but simply to earn a living and in effect help keep the economy ticking. That seems to me to suggest a need for government at the federal level to be extremely interested.
There are other goals that can be accomplished in the area of urban transit such as energy conservation, a goal that 1 think is very much before Canadians at this time.
Then there is the extreme cost of expressways. In other words, if we do not have adequate urban transit it means indirectly that we must continue to promote the use of the automobile from home to work and back. We have come to the realization that the means of providing channels for these automobiles to move on, expressways and major roads, is a major expenditure in terms of dollars, of environmental pollution, and of parking. A failure to recognize the need for urban transit is an admission that we accept the other option, which is to continue to promote the use of the automobile for this purpose.
If there is any doubt about the relationship of federal aid to urban transit for the ordinary urban taxpayer, I suggest it is not entirely different to the kind of expenditures that the federal government still makes for medicare, family allowances, and old age pensions, where the benefit can be felt in

March 3, 1977
National Transportation Act
the pocketbook of the individual taxpayer who lives in the urban community. His mode of urban transit is basic to his daily life. All levels of government must be involved, just as they are in medicare. Municipal governments must be involved in ensuring there are adequate hospitals in the area, while provincial and federal governments provide funding. I suggest no level of government can stand aside in this day and age from the needs of urban transit.
I should like to feel that it was in direct recognition of this need-in fact, specifically in recognition of this need-that this government, or that in office during the twenty-ninth parliament, decided in its wisdom during the last election campaign to recognize the need to make a commitment to the Canadian people that there would be substantial capital assistance to municipalities to assist them to acquire the much-needed new equipment to improve urban transit. 1 believe the commitment was somewhere in the area of $300 million. It is important to recognize that approximately one-third of this, $100 million, has already been put into this project and will start working its way into the system this spring. But that is not enough, Mr. Speaker. There must be recognition of the remainder of the commitment. I am pleased to note that on more than one occasion in the House during this past week in the question period the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicated that a decision on this has not been finalized. The cabinet is still considering the matter. I plead with it to look at this area of need, affecting ordinary citizens in the streets of our towns and cities, as it looks at other social services such as medicare, old age assistance, family allowances, etc., services which are basic to people's everyday lives.
It is important to discourage the use of vehicles which transport only one or two people to work, and to encourage the use of vehicles which will transport many people efficiently, save energy, and pollute the environment less. People will use rapid transit increasingly if it meets their needs, is clean, and efficient. They will not use it if it is inconvenient, for example if they must stand in the cold a long time waiting for a bus. Then they will say no, they will use their automobiles. The government can discourage the use of the automobile by providing services which will persuade people to switch to public transport.
Before leaving this topic I should like to refer to the reaction of certain municipal authorities to the announcement that the government's commitment in this area will possibly be curtailed this year. I note particularly the reaction of authorities in metropolitan Toronto. It disturbs me immensely to note that certain officials of metropolitan Toronto have indicated in the last ten days or two weeks that they are about to renege on their commitment to provide light, rapid transit for the borough of Scarborough. They do not help me in the case I am trying to make, that the federal government should contribute substantially to urban transit. It is unfortunate that municipal governments themselves cannot fix their policies, stay with them and stop equivocating. All the same I implore our federal authorities to remember their commitment. At the same time I

plead with elected municipal officials to carry out their plans for providing the urban transit system our people demand.
It has been said that we cannot afford new urban transit systems, that they are a luxury at this time. I say that the $200 million-odd which was committed to this area was not to be spent on a luxury. It was to fill a real need. In view of the large budgets of various departments and large loans made to various Crown corporations, and in view of the amounts provided in estimates for various government services, I suggest that we could meet needs in transportation by bringing about a small shift in the ordering of priorities. Surely in a budget of over $40 billion it should not be difficult to rearrange some of our priorities and keep a basic commitment made during the 1974 election campaign, for that would give the ordinary taxpayer the feeling that the federal governement is concerned about those things which affect most of us day in, day out.
I come now to inter-urban transit. It is time we developed an over-all strategy in this country for inter-urban transit. At present we have three basic modes of transportation, air, rail, and road. One way or another, we subsidize those three modes. We subsidize extensively the air and rail services, and subsidize indirectly bus services. We do not subsidize bus services directly, but subsidize the roads on which they run. I suggest that we need some sort of transport strategy in this area, and I put forward once more recommendations I made in other forums. I suggest that we should provide buses which would give clean, efficient, and fast service for trips up to 200 miles. We should set up appropriate bus depots to meet needs, so that people would be encouraged to use the bus for trips of up to 200 miles. In southwestern and eastern Ontario such bus trips would cover trips to many of our major centres. Unfortunately in Scarborough, an area with a population of 400,000, we do not even have a bus terminal. There is something irrational about that. We spend millions on new airports, but there is not even one bus terminal to serve a community of 400,000.
For trips between 200 and 500 miles we should use rail service. We should provide fast, efficient, and economical rail service for trips of up to 500 miles. We should encourage Canadians to use aircraft only for trips greater than 500 miles. We need a strategy which will take into account air, rail, and bus services and encourage the maximum possible use of each mode instead of encouraging competition between them in any given transport corridor.
I shall now deal with the safety factor at level crossings. This subject is of concern to many members representing urban areas where the exposure factor is high. By the exposure factor I mean the factor arrived at by multiplying the number of trains with the number of automobiles and other vehicles crossing any given point. Personally I am not satisfied that the Canadian Transport Commission has been tough enough in this area, and not satisfied that it has acted sufficiently in the public interest. There has not been enough insistence on meeting safety requirements at level crossings where there is a high exposure factor. I have had some personal experience in this matter, for in Scarborough, a municipality of 400,000,
March 3, 1977

there are 35 level crossings. It has taken me a whole year to convince the commission that a new examination of each of those level crossings is needed to determine if the current safety factors are adequate.
I am concerned, because there seems to be an inclination on the part of the regulatory body when considering these crossings to be very conscious of the needs of the railways. If a train is normally permitted to travel at 90 miles an hour through an urban area, there seems to be an extreme reluctance to suggest that the speed limit be reduced to 50 or 60 miles an hour where there are a number of dangerous level crossings. There does not seem to be the same degree of concern over the expressed concern of individual citizens. What 1 am attempting to say is that the safety factor for level crossings is too frequently looked upon by the regulatory body as something that is there to ensure satisfaction on the part of the railway.
I have one interesting and recent example. Signal lights were installed at an intersection in my borough. 1 discovered that the signal lights had not been installed primarily because of a demand by the people. They were installed because of a demand by the railway so that its trains could move through that intersection without them being obligated to post a flagman and conduct the train through.
It is this whole area where I feel the concerns of the public need to receive more attention on the part of the regulatory body than now is the case. I think the regulatory body must lay down its regulations once it has examined each and every situation, and insist that the railways as well as the public carry out those regulations and follow them.
Grade separations are becoming an increasingly difficult subject because of the increasing expense of each grade separation. It has been estimated in my own community that to separate 16 of the most urgent crossings at the present time would cost $69 million, of which the federal government would make by far the largest contribution.
All I ask at this time is that the minister, in bringing this bill forward, do nothing to damage in any way or otherwise affect the relocation fund that is currently available and from which money can be drawn when approved applications come forward from the municipalities and are approved by the Canadian Transport Commission as warranting a grade separation. I feel this particular fund is working. I am most concerned that nothing be done in the course of implementing this bill to affect in any way the provision of those kinds of finances.
I realize that all grade separations cannot be done at once. It is a slow and methodical process. However, with increasing attention to the safety factor at level crossings, and an increasing push to move all of these grade seperations as they come forward and finance them at the federal-provincial level, we can eventually accomplish them all.
My real concern is if this fund were to disappear or in any
way be transferred to another level of government to operate,
we would be in serious trouble. I plead with the minister to
National Transportation Act
ensure that, in this legislation at least, nothing will be done to give rise to any change in that particular type of funding.
Lastly, I want to speak of the role of the Canadian Transport Commission in those areas with which I am familiar. They are very limited, but they come from my own personal involvement. I have mentioned one, the matter of adequacy of safety standards.
There is another one to which I have addressed a private member's bill. It has received considerable support in this House and I trust it will continue to receive the support of the government as it goes through committee. I refer to the matter of requiring the railways to come before the CTC to have their plans for extension of marshalling yards or other facilities approved by the CTC before proceeding. This is an area where there is inadequate consideration of the concerns of the public.
I mentioned the need for the ordinary property owners in most urban areas across this country to go to their municipality when they wish to put up the lightest type of building in their own back yard. However, because they possess a right of way, the railways are not required to go to anybody when they wish to construct on that right of way, no matter what type of facility they want to construct. There is a requirement that they do this for new branch lines.
I have suggested in my private member's bill and I urge the government to take an increasing interest in policy as a result of this bill, that when the railways have construction plans they should insist that they bring them before a public body, giving the neighbours in that particular community an opportunity to present themselves and speak in support of or against a particular proposal.
I urge the minister, in redirecting some of the responsibilities of the Canadian Transport Commission, to insist that it indeed become a body to serve the public and to be seen by the public as an instrument acting in their individual interest.
These are several remarks that I wish to address in connection with this particular bill. In some ways they are unrelated, but, in my view, all important. They all express the concern 1 have about the need of government to be active itself in transportation problems associated with people rather than with goods. I realize the problems in the area of goods, but this time I am addressing myself specifically to problems involving people.
I ask once again for further consideration of this commitment to aid for urban transit, bearing in mind that it is an area that is felt individually by each worker every day of his life as he goes back and forth to work. It is as important to him as having proper hospitalization, proper provision for his old age, proper assistance for other things over which he has no control.
I intend to support this bill. However, again I ask the minister to use his persuasive powers with his government colleagues on those matters to which I addressed myself tonight, as did my other colleagues, particularly those from the urban areas of Toronto and Montreal.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-SOVIET UNION-INQUIRY WHETFIER REPRESENTATIONS MADE BY MINISTER FOR RELEASE OF GEORGI VINS
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-SOVIET UNION-INQUIRY WHETFIER REPRESENTATIONS MADE BY MINISTER FOR RELEASE OF GEORGI VINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to bring to the attention of the House tonight a topic that has received much publicity of recent date. That is the matter of the internment of prisoners of conscience in the USSR. Specifically I want to raise the case of one Georgi Vins.
In August, 1975, when the Helsinki accord was signed, and especially when the third basket was signed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), along with the other leaders, I am sure most of us were filled with the hope that peace, stability, and specifically the recognition of human rights, would be upheld by the nations represented at the signing of the Helsinki accord. Moreover, human rights are guaranteed under article 18 of the United Nations Declaration on Human Rights.
But despite the signing of the Helsinki accord, prisoners of conscience in the USSR have spent time in Soviet prisons, they have spent time in labour camps, generally in Siberia, and further, as one of the most invidious forms of punishment ever devised, they have spent time in psychiatric institutions, hidden from the eyes of the world and hidden from international justice. The prisoner I want to mention today, Mr. Georgi Vins, is serving time for a crime no more serious than that of practising his religious faith. That is a crime in the USSR.
On November 14, 1976, I moved a motion under Standing Order 43 as follows:
That members of this House urge the Prime Minister to make representations to the government of the USSR that Georgi Vins be released from imprisonment and that the government of the Soviet Union allow him and all other religious believers within its borders to worship God freely according to their own consciences, as the Soviet Union is committed to do by the provisions of its constitution and by the provisions of the United Nations covenant on civil and political rights which the Soviet Union has ratified.
That motion was denied unanimous consent. On the same day I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) whether he would make specific representations to the USSR on behalf of Mr. Vins, a Baptist pastor in the
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner).]
March 3, 1977
USSR who was arrested in March, 1974, for professing his faith and sentenced on June 28, 1975, to five years' imprisonment, plus an additional five years in exile, plus confiscation of property, a penalty which directly affects his family and, specifically, his five children. His offence? Teaching the Bible to those under the age of 18 and leading what was termed an unorganized religious group. He was tried under section 209 of the criminal code of the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic.
The World Council of Churches has written to the USSR, saying in part:
We have reason to believe, on the basis of information received, that the charges against Mr. Vins are made primarily because of his religious convictions and activities.
The Nobel prizewinner, Andrei Sakharov, wrote:
The arrests, breaking-up of prayer meetings, fines, discrimination in school and at work, and, as the height of inhumanity, the taking away of children from their parents all this is the lot of the Baptist and to one degree or another of many other religious groups who arc inconvenient to the authorities.
What is to happen? World opinion today cannot allow itself to lessen its moral support for these prisoners of conscience. Western news media must focus attention on the struggle for human rights in the USSR, and we, as parliamentarians, must stand up and say that what is happening in the Soviet Union is wrong. When the Prime Minister went to see President Carter I was tremendously pleased with the direct approach the President had taken. Yet it was evident from the reply of the Secretary of State for External Affairs that direct representations on behalf of Georgi Vins have not been made.
The Prime Minister said this week that we intend to follow the diplomatic route rather than the direct route. I have not had time to explain the case in detail, but I want to say that what we as Canadians have done is not enough. What the Prime Minister has done is not enough. What we as parliamentarians have done is not enough.
The Helsinki accord is a farce in the USSR. It has been a total and absolute abdication of what the USSR authorities signed. The families of these men and women, and in many , many cases their blood, cry out for justice. I urge, I plead, that the Prime Minister, his officials, and for that matter all parliamentarians, stand up and voice the concern of a concerned world that human rights are being severely violated in the USSR, and that international world opinion demands a radical change of attitude and justice for these many people who are victims of a very, very cruel regime.

subtopic: MANPOWER-GRANTS TO CONSTITUENCIES IN RESPECT OF MANPOWER MOBILITY
MANPOWER-GRANTS TO CONSTITUENCIES IN RESPECT OF MANPOWER MOBILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize for detaining the House at such a late hour. However, I am exercising an ancient and important right on behalf of a citizen who, I am sure the House will agree, has fallen into difficulty through no fault of his own.
I wish to compliment the minister and his department for taking action. After 1 gave his office notice of the question, the minister was good enough to have one of his officials give my constituent, Mr. Carlton Champion, landed immigrant status after almost six years in this country, four X-ray examinations, all of which were sent by registered mail to the department, and two other applications.
Unhappily, the department lost my constituent's file. The department alleges that my constituent moved too often. In fact he moved from the United States to Toronto, and from Toronto to Goose Bay, Labrador, where he was employed by one of the agencies of the government of Canada. His neighbour on one side was an immigration officer and so was his neighbour across the street, friends and acquaintances of his. He was registered with Manpower at Goose Bay and was registered with the immigration service at Goose Bay, so there was no question of any hiding. My constituent also underwent a security check with the government of Canada which included fingerprinting, so any question that he was avoiding publicizing where he was, is totally inaccurate. He was an employee of this government and of the Public Service of Canada.
Adjournment Debate
In any event, the files were lost. My constituent came to this country in August of 1971, but only last week was a ministerial permit issued authorizing him to be in Canada, despite the fact that I have in front of me a letter from the Department of Manpower and Immigration dated August 12, 1971, Toronto, which reads:
Wc have received an application for permanent admission to Canada from Mr. Carlton Champion. There is no objection on our pari to the above named accepting employment, pending compliance with immigration requirements.
Yours very truly.
It was signed for the district administrator of Canada Immigration Centre. The problem is that because his status was only settled last week, my constituent was ineligible for a manpower mobility payment. His wife and four children are in severely destitute circumstances. Here I want to pay another compliment to the department, the immigration people m Saint-John, New-Brunswick, who were so upset at the way this case has been handled that they have seen to it that my constituent has work. He has now returned to work for one of the government agencies. Unhappily, it is only for six weeks. But my constituent, who was at Goose Bay, Labrador, when the Goose Bay facility was phased out, had to move to Saint John, New Brunswick. He was told that he would be eligible for manpower mobility funding, and when it was discovered that his status, through no fault of his, had not been cleared up and he was still a stateless person until last week, he was denied manpower mobility funding.
I am exercising on his part his privilege, one 1 am glad to undertake, because 1 am sure that a sensitive and sympathetic department would wish, as I do, to go the second mile in unravelling this complicated and quite heartrending case. The department has solved the status issue about five years too late because my constituent will now have to wait three years, as 1 understand it, before claiming his right to citizenship, instead of being a citizen now, as he would have been if the department has not lost his file. He also, unhappily, has his furniture in storage. It is about to be re-possessed. I have gone to the trouble of sending a telegram asking the movers to hold up on selling the furniture until a sensitive, compassionate department can do what it should do on behalf of Carlton Champion and see to it that the manpower mobility payment is paid.

subtopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS-LOG HOUSING PROGRAM FOR NORTHERN CANADA
NORTHERN AFFAIRS-LOG HOUSING PROGRAM FOR NORTHERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have this opportunity to raise once again a matter which is of great importance. I have mentioned this matter in this House many times. I have raised it in public and in committee.
Generally speaking, I have found agreement with this idea.
It is not a new one. It is one I have been pursuing for sometime, and I have been trying to get some response from the government. I have been trying to get the government to take the initiative whereby a good housing program can be put into place in the Northwest Territories, especially in the Mackenzie district. I have been advocating a good log housing program under which people can build their own homes in the Mackenzie district using a local renewable resource, namely, logs, which are in abundance, especially along the Mackenzie and in the Liard area. I think this idea makes sense for the simple reason that a good log housing program would make use of a local, renewable, natural resource. It would provide badly needed jobs, and it would also provide housing for people in the Mackenzie district.
I have described the area at other times in this place as a disaster area, and that it is. I know this because I have travelled in the Mackenzie district. I have travelled in many parts of the Northwest Territories for many years. As hon. members know, I canvassed door to door in my campaign to become elected to the House of Commons.
I am raising this question again because I have not been able to get a positive response from the department. As most people know, bad housing creates social problems. Children do not do well in school, young people in the family may not be able to hold jobs, there are health problems, and there are

mental health problems, especially, in a very, very, cold climate. For some time I have been advocating that the territorial administration, through the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, initiate a good log housing program in the Mackenzie district of the Northwest Territories. People there who already have good log houses know that they will last for 100 years or more. As a rule maintenance is minimal and, as the houses are generally well insulated, heating does not cost a lot. Not much training is needed for construction, and I think we already have enough people with the knowledge to establish a good program. The need is there the material is there, and the labour is there.
If the program were launched it could start by filling an immediate need of the legislature of the Northwest Territories. They have a table, they have chairs for the members to sit on, a mace, and recently a Speaker's chair was presented by the Parliament of Canada to the legislature of the Northwest Territories. But, Mr. Speaker, they do not have a building. I suggest a project could be launched through Canada Works, perhaps the Department of Regional Economic Expansion or some leftover funds from LIP programs, and a log building constructed to house the Speaker's chair, the table, chairs, and mace that the legislature already has. Maybe 50 or 100 years from now the people of the territories would want a different kind of building, but this would be a starting point for a log housing program.
I may be stepping out of line, Mr. Speaker, in suggesting that some of the municipalities in the territories change their regulations that forbid a certain style of log construction The decision is up to them, but I would hope, once it was shown that a good log house worked and fitted in with the environment, that the regulations would be changed.
I should like to ask the department what the government is doing about such a program. I am sure this is not the first time they have heard about it and I will see to it that they hear more about it in the future. Is the government doing anything about such an idea?

speakeroldname: Mr. B. Keith Penner (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS-LOG HOUSING PROGRAM FOR NORTHERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the 1972 recommendations of the Northwest Territories Council task force on housing, all of the provincial type housing responsibilities were transferred by the department to the territorial government. In 1974 the N.W.T. Housing Corporation assumed these responsibilities.
The housing corporation has made the greatest possible use of the various housing programs provided by the National Housing Act. Due to the particular needs of the many low income residents of the territories, the public housing program, under sections 40 and 43 of the National Housing Act, have provided most of the family accommodation built to date.
Following Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation's agreement to provide NHA loans for the capital costs and to share in the operating losses of any approved log houses included in the public housing program, the N.W.T. Housing Corporation established a log milling operation in Fort Resolu-

tion. Local labour and materials were utilized to produce uniform sized logs which would meet CMHC standards. To date 37 log houses have been completed and ten more are under construction in various communities in the Mackenzie River area. The per unit costs have ranged from S50,000 to $77,000.
Unfortunately a major problem has been encountered. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation standards for the public housing program require logs of a minimum diameter of ten inches. The supply of trees of a size which will produce milled logs of this size is so limited that the inclusion of log houses in the public housing programs will end when the ones presently under construction are completed.
Although it is not limited to log housing, the N.W.T. Housing Corporation's "Small Settlement Home Assistance Program" encourages residents of smaller communities to utilize local materials, normally logs, for the construction of their homes. Any sized logs can be used in this program. The program has been providing grants of up to $5,000 to cover the cost of manufactured components, such as doors, windows,
Adjournment Debate
roofing, etc., required to complete a basic structure built of local materials. The housing corporation intends to increase the grants to a maximum of $10,000, including $7,500 for materials and $2,500 for transportation. The number of grants provided by the program is expected to increase from 20 in 1976-77 to 30 in each of the following years.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation's rural and remote housing program will be available for the first time in the Northwest Territories in 1977-78. The program's allowance for labour contributed by an applicant should encourage the use of logs for the basic house structure. Groups of residents in Fort Smith and in Fort Simpson have already applied for loans to construct log houses in those communities.
If only wood is used as fuel, any sized log can be used to build houses under this program.
